recipes.goal: You deliver a short presentation (roughly 5 to 15 minutes) that lands one clear message with an audience, delivered on time and without technical mishaps.

steps.action: **Decide the one message.** Finish this sentence: "If they remember only one thing, it is ___." Everything serves that sentence.
steps.expect: a single message written in one line.

steps.action: **Structure with the rule of three.** Three supporting points, no more; audiences hold three well and forget five. Open by stating the message, cover the three, close by restating it.
steps.expect: an outline of exactly three points bracketed by the message.

steps.action: **Build spare slides (if any).** Roughly one idea per slide, large text, few words, a strong visual over a wall of bullets. Slides support you; they are not your script.
steps.expect: slides readable from the back row, none crammed.

steps.action: **Rehearse aloud, out loud, on your feet.** Reading silently hides the stumbles; speaking reveals timing and awkward transitions. Time it.
steps.expect: two full run-throughs, and a measured runtime under your limit with margin.

steps.action: **Cut to fit with margin.** Aim for ~80% of the allotted time; overruns are the most common and most resented failure.
steps.expect: rehearsed runtime comfortably inside the limit.

steps.action: **Do a full tech check in the actual setup.** Connect your laptop to the real projector or join the actual call; test the adapter, clicker, sound, and screen-share. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* a live failure cannot be redone, so verify the adapter and have slides exported to PDF on a USB stick and emailed to yourself as backups.
steps.expect: your first slide displays on the real screen and the clicker advances it.

steps.action: **Deliver: open strong, watch the audience, close on the message.** Make eye contact, slow down (nerves speed you up), and end by restating the one message rather than trailing into "so, yeah, that's it."
steps.expect: you finish on time with a clean restatement, then invite questions.

recipes.verification: You delivered within the time limit, stated your one message at both the open and close, the visuals displayed correctly (or you adapted cleanly), and the audience can repeat your core message back.

recipes.title: give difficult feedback to a report
recipes.name: give-difficult-feedback-to-a-report
recipes.goal: Give difficult feedback to a direct report in a way that is specific, fair, documented, and tied to future expectations.

steps.action: **Prepare examples.** Write observable facts, dates, work artifacts, and impacts, avoiding labels like "lazy" or "negative."
steps.expect: feedback is evidence-based.

steps.action: **Check severity.** Decide whether this is coaching, formal performance feedback, policy issue, or urgent risk.
steps.expect: you know whether HR or another process is needed.

steps.action: **Schedule privately.** Set a private meeting soon after the relevant event, with enough time for discussion.
steps.expect: the report is not surprised in public.

steps.action: **State the issue directly.** Say, "I need to discuss a pattern in missed handoff deadlines and its impact on the launch team."
steps.expect: the topic is clear early.

steps.action: **Describe behavior and impact.** Use "When X happened, Y was affected" and pause for their perspective.
steps.expect: the report understands the gap.

steps.action: **Listen for context.** [BRANCH: skill gap | motivation issue | external blocker] offer training for skill gaps; clarify expectations for motivation issues; remove or escalate blockers where real.
steps.expect: response matches cause.

steps.action: **Set future expectations.** Define what good looks like, by when, and how progress will be checked.
steps.expect: the report knows how to recover.

steps.action: **Document the conversation.** Send a concise recap with examples, expectations, support offered, and follow-up date.
steps.expect: both sides have a fair record.

recipes.verification: The report receives specific examples, impact, expected future behavior, support offered, follow-up date, and written recap appropriate to the issue's severity.

recipes.title: handle an angry customer
recipes.name: handle-an-angry-customer
recipes.goal: Respond to an angry customer in a way that lowers tension, captures the issue, sets realistic next steps, and protects the business relationship.

steps.action: **Regulate your response.** Pause, use a steady tone, and avoid matching the customer's volume or sarcasm.
steps.expect: you can respond professionally.

steps.action: **Acknowledge the emotion and issue.** Say, "I can hear how frustrating this has been, and I want to understand what happened."
steps.expect: the customer hears recognition before problem-solving.

steps.action: **Gather facts.** Ask for order number, date, product, impact, prior contacts, and desired resolution.
steps.expect: the complaint becomes specific.

steps.action: **Confirm understanding.** Summarize: "You were charged twice on August 12 and still cannot access the account."
steps.expect: the customer can correct or confirm the facts.

steps.action: **State what you can do now.** [BRANCH: authorized resolution | escalation needed] offer the approved fix if authorized; explain escalation path, owner, and timeline if not.
steps.expect: next steps are realistic.

steps.action: **Set boundaries if needed.** Say, "I want to help, but I cannot continue if you insult or threaten staff."
steps.expect: abusive behavior has a clear limit.

steps.action: **Document the interaction.** Record facts, promises, policy references, and emotional or safety concerns in the case system.
steps.expect: the next person has context.

steps.action: **Follow up when promised.** Send a recap with case number, resolution path, deadline, and contact channel.
steps.expect: the customer has a written record.

recipes.verification: The case record contains the customer's issue, confirmed facts, offered resolution or escalation, promised timeline, and any boundary or safety notes.

recipes.title: introduce yourself professionally
recipes.name: introduce-yourself-professionally
recipes.goal: Prepare and deliver a professional self-introduction that states your name, role, value, context, and handoff in about 20 seconds.

steps.action: **Identify the context.** Decide whether the introduction is for networking, a meeting, an interview, or a new team.
steps.expect: the tone and detail level are clear.

steps.action: **Write the name-role-value line.** Combine your name, role or background, and the useful thing you bring.
steps.expect: one sentence explains who you are.

steps.action: **Add one context detail.** Mention the project, team, problem, or reason you are in the conversation.
steps.expect: the listener understands why you are relevant now.

steps.action: **Keep it to 20 seconds.** Aim for 3 or 4 sentences, roughly 40 to 60 spoken words.
steps.expect: it feels complete but not like a speech.

steps.action: **Tailor the wording.** [BRANCH: formal | casual | interview] adjust title, detail, and warmth to the setting.
steps.expect: the introduction fits the room.

steps.action: **Prepare the handoff.** End with a question, next person cue, or reason you are looking forward to the discussion.
steps.expect: conversation can continue naturally.

steps.action: **Practice aloud twice.** Listen for jargon, rambling, or details that require too much explanation.
steps.expect: the wording sounds spoken, not memorized text.

steps.action: **Deliver with basics.** Say your name clearly, make brief eye contact or camera contact, and stop after the handoff.
steps.expect: the listener can repeat your name and role.

steps.action: **Adapt after response.** If they ask a follow-up, expand with one relevant example rather than restarting the introduction.
steps.expect: the conversation moves forward.

recipes.verification: Your introduction can be spoken in about 20 seconds and includes name, role or background, value, tailored context, and a clear handoff.

recipes.title: leave a voicemail
recipes.name: leave-a-voicemail
recipes.goal: You leave a short, clear voicemail that tells the listener who called, why, and how and when to reach you back, in under 30 seconds.

steps.action: **Plan the message before it beeps.** Jot four things: your name, your number, the reason, the callback window.
steps.expect: a four-point note in front of you.

steps.action: **Wait for the beep, then greet and name yourself immediately.** "Hi, this is [full name] calling for [person/office]."
steps.expect: your name is the first content, not buried after rambling.

steps.action: **State your phone number slowly, early.** Say it digit by digit at dictation speed.
steps.expect: a listener could write it down on first hearing.

steps.action: **Give the reason in one or two sentences.** Concrete and specific: what you need and any reference number.
steps.expect: the listener knows why you called without guessing.

steps.action: **State when you are reachable (the callback window).** "I'm available today until 5 p.m., or tomorrow morning."
steps.expect: the listener knows a good time, reducing phone tag.

steps.action: **Repeat your name and number a second time at the end.** This is the one repetition that matters; the listener may have missed it the first time.
steps.expect: name and number given exactly twice, bookending the message.

steps.action: **Close and hang up cleanly.** "Thanks, again this is [name] at [number]. Talk soon." Press end; do not trail off.
steps.expect: message ends crisply, total length under ~30 seconds.

recipes.verification: The message is under ~30 seconds and contains, in order, your name, number (spoken slowly), a clear reason, a callback window, and a closing repeat of name and number.

recipes.title: make a complaint call
recipes.name: make-a-complaint-call
recipes.goal: You reach a company or service by phone, state a complaint clearly and calmly, and obtain a concrete resolution or a documented path to one.

steps.action: **Assemble evidence before dialing.** Order number, dates, amounts, prior email/chat references, and a one-sentence statement of what went wrong and what you want.
steps.expect: a short written list you can read from under pressure.

steps.action: **Define your target outcome and your fallback.** E.g. "full refund" with a fallback of "credit plus fee waiver".
steps.expect: two acceptable outcomes written down before you call.

steps.action: **Call and navigate the menu to a human.** Note the time you called. Pressing 0, saying "agent", or choosing "cancel service" often routes to a person fastest.
steps.expect: connected to or queued for a live representative.

steps.action: **Get the agent's name and location at the start.** "Who am I speaking with, and can I get a reference number for this call?"
steps.expect: a name and, ideally, a case/ticket number written in your notes.

steps.action: **State the complaint in three parts: what happened, the impact, what you want.** Keep it factual and brief; then stop talking and let them respond.
steps.expect: the agent restates the issue and begins working it.

steps.action: **Stay calm and firm; separate the problem from the person.** The agent did not cause it and can be your ally. If you feel anger rising, slow your speech rather than raise your voice.
steps.expect: a working, cooperative tone; the agent proposes a resolution or next step.

steps.action: **If the answer is inadequate, climb the escalation ladder.** Ask: "I understand your limit here. May I speak with a supervisor?" Note each name and time.
steps.expect: transfer to someone with more authority, or a firm commitment with a reference number.

steps.action: **Confirm and log the resolution.** Repeat back the agreed action, amount, and timeframe, and ask for written confirmation by email.
steps.expect: a clear commitment (who, what, by when) plus a case number and a promised email.

recipes.verification: You have a written record of the call (agent name, time, case number) and either a completed resolution or a specific commitment with a date, ideally confirmed by a follow-up email.

recipes.title: mediate a conflict between coworkers
recipes.name: mediate-a-conflict-between-coworkers
recipes.goal: Mediate a workplace conflict so coworkers can agree on facts, impacts, boundaries, and next working agreements.

steps.action: **Screen for escalation needs.** Check whether the conflict involves threats, harassment, discrimination, retaliation, or policy violations.
steps.expect: serious issues are routed before informal mediation.

steps.action: **Talk to each person separately.** Ask each coworker what happened, what impact it had, and what outcome they want.
steps.expect: you understand each perspective before convening.

steps.action: **Set meeting rules.** State that the conversation will use observable facts, impact statements, no interruptions, and future-focused requests.
steps.expect: the discussion has boundaries.

steps.action: **Name the shared problem.** Phrase the issue as "The handoff process is failing" rather than "Alex is careless."
steps.expect: the conversation targets work behavior.

steps.action: **Let each person speak.** Give each coworker uninterrupted time to describe facts and impact.
steps.expect: both feel heard before problem-solving.

steps.action: **Identify agreements and gaps.** Separate facts both accept from interpretations still in dispute.
steps.expect: the group knows what must be solved.

steps.action: **Create working agreements.** [BRANCH: process conflict | interpersonal conflict] define handoff, review, or decision rules for process conflict; define communication boundaries for interpersonal conflict.
steps.expect: future behavior is specific.

steps.action: **Document follow-up.** Send a neutral recap with agreements, owners, dates, and escalation path if agreements fail.
steps.expect: accountability does not depend on memory.

recipes.verification: Both coworkers receive a neutral written recap that lists agreed behaviors, owners, follow-up date, and escalation path if the agreement is not followed.

recipes.title: negotiate a job offer
recipes.name: negotiate-a-job-offer
recipes.goal: Negotiate a job offer respectfully by getting terms in writing, evaluating the whole package, countering clearly, managing deadlines, and closing gracefully.

steps.action: **Get the offer in writing.** Ask for salary, bonus, equity, benefits, start date, title, manager, location, and deadline.
steps.expect: the negotiable terms are visible in one document or email.

steps.action: **Evaluate the whole package.** Include base pay, bonus probability, equity terms, insurance, retirement, time off, remote policy, commute, and growth.
steps.expect: you know the real value and tradeoffs.

steps.action: **Pick negotiation priorities.** Choose 1 to 3 items that matter most, such as base salary, signing bonus, start date, or remote days.
steps.expect: the counter is focused.

steps.action: **Ground the counter.** Use market data, competing constraints, experience, or role scope to justify the request.
steps.expect: the employer hears a business reason, not a demand.

steps.action: **Write the counter respectfully.** State enthusiasm, ask for specific changes, and invite discussion.
steps.expect: the tone preserves the relationship.

steps.action: **Manage the deadline.** If you need time, ask for an extension before the deadline and give a reason.
steps.expect: the employer confirms the active decision window.

steps.action: **Review the revised offer.** [BRANCH: improved | unchanged | worse] compare every term against the original and your minimum.
steps.expect: you know whether to accept, counter again, or decline.

steps.action: **Accept only in writing.** Confirm the final terms and start date before resigning from a current job. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* resignation and relocation decisions can be costly, so confirm final written terms first.
steps.expect: the accepted offer matches what you agreed.

steps.action: **Decline gracefully if needed.** Thank them, state you are declining, and avoid criticism or unnecessary detail.
steps.expect: the relationship remains professional.

recipes.verification: You have a final written offer or written decline record that reflects the negotiated terms, deadline handling, and professional close.

recipes.title: negotiate with a vendor
recipes.name: negotiate-with-a-vendor
recipes.goal: Negotiate with a vendor to improve price, terms, scope, risk allocation, or service without damaging the working relationship.

steps.action: **Define your walk-away point.** Identify maximum price, required terms, and acceptable alternatives.
steps.expect: you know your limits before negotiating.

steps.action: **Separate needs from preferences.** Mark requirements such as data security, uptime, delivery date, or legal clauses apart from nice-to-haves.
steps.expect: concessions are deliberate.

steps.action: **Research leverage.** Compare market pricing, competing vendors, usage data, renewal timing, and vendor incentives.
steps.expect: requests are grounded in evidence.

steps.action: **Open collaboratively.** Say, "We want to make this work, but we need the proposal to fit our budget and security requirements."
steps.expect: the tone is firm without hostility.

steps.action: **Make specific asks.** Request exact changes: discount, payment schedule, service credits, termination right, implementation support, or scope adjustment.
steps.expect: the vendor can respond concretely.

steps.action: **Trade, do not concede silently.** [BRANCH: price issue | terms issue] exchange longer commitment or reference call for price; exchange narrower scope or controls for terms.
steps.expect: every concession gets value back.

steps.action: **Confirm in writing.** Summarize agreed terms, open points, deadlines, and who must approve.
steps.expect: negotiation history is clear.

steps.action: **Route final documents.** Send the contract or quote through procurement, finance, legal, or security before signature.
steps.expect: internal approval happens before commitment.

recipes.verification: The final vendor agreement reflects written price, scope, service, timing, risk terms, and required internal approvals before anyone signs or pays.

recipes.title: onboard to a new job
recipes.name: onboard-to-a-new-job
recipes.goal: Start a new job with a clear operating map: people, tools, expectations, first deliverables, and communication norms.

steps.action: **Confirm first-week logistics.** Ask where to be, when to arrive or log in, what equipment to bring, and what accounts should work.
steps.expect: you know the first-day plan.

steps.action: **Set up your workspace.** Configure email, calendar, chat, password manager, payroll, HR, device security, and required team tools.
steps.expect: you can receive messages and access core systems.

steps.action: **Build a people map.** List your manager, teammates, cross-functional partners, onboarding buddy, HR contact, and IT support.
steps.expect: you know who handles common questions.

steps.action: **Clarify success measures.** Ask your manager, "What would make my first 30 days useful to the team?"
steps.expect: success is defined in outcomes, not only meetings attended.

steps.action: **Learn communication norms.** Ask which decisions go in chat, email, tickets, docs, and meetings.
steps.expect: you can choose the right channel for routine work.

steps.action: **Create a question list.** Group open questions by product, people, process, and permissions.
steps.expect: you can batch questions instead of interrupting constantly.

steps.action: **Deliver a small early win.** [BRANCH: assigned task | no assigned task] complete the assigned starter task; if none exists, ask for a low-risk documentation, bug, or analysis task.
steps.expect: you contribute something visible and bounded.

steps.action: **Send a first-week recap.** Send your manager a note with what you learned, what is blocked, and what you plan next.
steps.expect: expectations are aligned before habits harden.

recipes.verification: You can name your top priorities, key contacts, required tools, first deliverable, and next check-in date without guessing.

recipes.title: pitch an idea to your boss
recipes.name: pitch-an-idea-to-your-boss
recipes.goal: Pitch an idea to your boss with a clear problem, business value, costs, risks, and specific decision request.

steps.action: **Define the problem.** Write one sentence naming who is affected, what is happening, and why it matters.
steps.expect: the idea starts from a real need.

steps.action: **Describe the proposal.** State the idea in plain language and avoid solution jargon.
steps.expect: your boss can repeat the idea after one read.

steps.action: **Estimate value and effort.** Include expected benefit, required people, cost, timeline, and tradeoffs.
steps.expect: the pitch feels practical.

steps.action: **Address risks.** Name likely objections such as budget, priority, adoption, compliance, or maintenance.
steps.expect: concerns are anticipated rather than ignored.

steps.action: **Ask for a specific decision.** Use "I'm asking for approval to spend two weeks validating this with three customers."
steps.expect: the next action is clear.

steps.action: **Choose the format.** [BRANCH: quick idea | significant investment] use a short message for a small test; use a one-page brief and meeting for significant investment.
steps.expect: pitch size matches decision size.

steps.action: **Invite critique.** Ask "What would need to be true for this to be worth trying?"
steps.expect: feedback improves the proposal.

steps.action: **Follow up in writing.** Send the decision, open questions, and next step after the conversation.
steps.expect: momentum does not depend on memory.

recipes.verification: Your boss receives a concise pitch that states problem, proposal, value, cost, risks, and a specific requested decision or next step.

recipes.title: prepare for a performance review
recipes.name: prepare-for-a-performance-review
recipes.goal: Prepare for a performance review with evidence, a clear self-assessment, and specific asks for growth, compensation, or support.

steps.action: **Collect evidence.** Gather goals, shipped work, metrics, stakeholder notes, and examples of collaboration or leadership.
steps.expect: you have a fact base instead of relying on memory.

steps.action: **Map evidence to expectations.** Match each accomplishment to role expectations, team goals, or business outcomes.
steps.expect: your review story shows why the work mattered.

steps.action: **Write your self-assessment.** Use this structure: "This period I delivered X, which changed Y; I learned Z; next I want to improve A."
steps.expect: the draft is concise and evidence-backed.

steps.action: **Name misses honestly.** List 1-3 areas where outcomes, communication, or execution could have been better, plus what changed.
steps.expect: weaknesses are framed as owned learning, not excuses.

steps.action: **Prepare your asks.** [BRANCH: growth | compensation] ask for specific projects, feedback, or scope for growth; ask about process, timing, and criteria for compensation.
steps.expect: you know what you want from the conversation.

steps.action: **Rehearse hard questions.** Practice answers to "What was your biggest miss?", "What support do you need?", and "Why do you think you are ready for more?"
steps.expect: you can answer directly without rambling.

steps.action: **Send supporting notes.** Share your self-assessment or agenda before the meeting if your review process allows it.
steps.expect: your manager can review evidence before giving feedback.

steps.action: **Capture outcomes after the review.** Write down feedback, commitments, dates, and open questions within the same day.
steps.expect: the conversation becomes an action plan.

recipes.verification: Your review packet includes accomplishments, misses, learned themes, and 2-3 explicit asks, and the post-review notes list owner, action, and date for each commitment.

recipes.title: quit a job gracefully
recipes.name: quit-a-job-gracefully
recipes.goal: A resignation is communicated clearly, professionally, and with a handover that protects your reputation and the team's continuity.

steps.action: **Review obligations first.** Check contract, employee handbook, offer letter, and local rules for notice, equipment, confidentiality, and repayment clauses.
steps.expect: you know the practical consequences before speaking.

steps.action: **Tell your manager first.** Request a private conversation and say directly that you are resigning and when your last day will be.
steps.expect: your manager hears it from you, not gossip or a system notice.

steps.action: **Keep the reason brief.** Share a simple explanation if you want, but do not litigate every frustration in the resignation meeting.
steps.expect: the conversation stays controlled.

steps.action: **Send the letter.** Put resignation, final day, thanks, and willingness to support transition in a short written note.
steps.expect: HR and your manager have a clear record.

steps.action: **Plan the handover.** [BRANCH: project role | people manager] List active work, deadlines, contacts, files, decisions, and risks; if you manage people, add review cycles and sensitive follow-ups.
steps.expect: the team can see what needs coverage.

steps.action: **Stay professional through notice.** Finish agreed tasks, document status, and avoid badmouthing the company or recruiting coworkers into your exit mood.
steps.expect: your last weeks support your future references.

steps.action: **Return property and access.** Confirm equipment, badges, accounts, expenses, and benefits paperwork. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* deleting files, taking confidential data, or burning access can create legal and career consequences, so separate personal materials carefully.
steps.expect: offboarding is clean.

steps.action: **Say goodbye well.** Thank key people, share personal contact information selectively, and leave concise notes for whoever inherits the work.
steps.expect: relationships survive the departure.

recipes.verification: Your manager and HR have written notice, final day is documented, handover materials exist, and company property and access are addressed.

recipes.title: request time off
recipes.name: request-time-off
recipes.goal: Request time off with enough notice, coverage, and written clarity that your manager can approve it without chasing details.

steps.action: **Check policy and balance.** Confirm whether the time is vacation, sick, personal, unpaid, bereavement, parental, or holiday time.
steps.expect: you know what category and amount you are requesting.

steps.action: **Check the calendar.** Look for launches, deadlines, team coverage gaps, holidays, and your manager's absence.
steps.expect: you can flag conflicts before your manager does.

steps.action: **Choose coverage.** Identify who can handle urgent issues, meetings, approvals, or on-call duties while you are out. [BRANCH: routine vacation | sensitive leave] give normal coverage for routine vacation; share only necessary details for medical or family leave.
steps.expect: the request includes a workable backup.

steps.action: **Give notice early.** Ask as soon as dates are likely, especially around holidays or long absences.
steps.expect: the team has time to plan.

steps.action: **Write the request plainly.** Include exact dates, return date, leave type if needed, coverage plan, and any deadlines you will finish before leaving.
steps.expect: the manager can approve from the message alone.

steps.action: **Submit in the required system.** Use the HR tool, calendar, email, or manager channel your workplace requires.
steps.expect: the request exists in writing and in the official place.

steps.action: **Prepare the handoff.** Before leaving, send a short note with status, owners, links, risks, and what can wait.
steps.expect: coworkers can cover without decoding your brain.

steps.action: **Set boundaries while away.** Update calendar, status, autoresponder if appropriate, and notification settings. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* nonrefundable travel or commitments should wait until leave is approved unless you accept the risk.
steps.expect: people can see you are out and know who to contact.

recipes.verification: The time off is approved or acknowledged in writing, appears on the relevant calendar or system, and has a visible coverage plan.

recipes.title: respond to a negative review
recipes.name: respond-to-a-negative-review
recipes.goal: A public response to a negative review that acknowledges the customer, protects the business's credibility, and moves detailed repair offline.

steps.action: **Pause before replying.** Read the review twice and wait until you can answer without arguing.
steps.expect: the response is professional, not reactive.

steps.action: **Verify what you can.** Check order, appointment, staff notes, photos, or policies without exposing private details.
steps.expect: you know whether apology, clarification, or investigation is needed.

steps.action: **Thank the reviewer.** Open with a brief thank-you for feedback, even if the review feels unfair.
steps.expect: readers see respect before defense.

steps.action: **Acknowledge the concern.** Name the issue in neutral language: wait time, damaged item, billing confusion, rude interaction, or missed expectation.
steps.expect: the reviewer can tell you read the actual complaint.

steps.action: **Apologize where due.** Say sorry for the experience or for the specific failure you can confirm.
steps.expect: responsibility is taken without inventing facts.

steps.action: **Offer to fix offline.** [BRANCH: known customer | unknown reviewer] If you can identify them, invite them to contact a named channel; if not, ask them to reach out with details.
steps.expect: private information leaves the public thread.

steps.action: **Keep it short and final.** Do not debate, reveal records, mention bans, or accuse the reviewer publicly. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* public replies can be screenshotted and amplified, so write for future customers as much as the reviewer.
steps.expect: the response improves trust even if the rating remains.

steps.action: **Log the issue internally.** Record the review, response, owner, and follow-up task.
steps.expect: the complaint can lead to operational repair.

recipes.verification: The public response thanks the reviewer, acknowledges the issue, apologizes where appropriate, offers offline follow-up, and avoids private details.

recipes.title: respond to a recruiter
recipes.name: respond-to-a-recruiter
recipes.goal: Respond to a recruiter clearly, whether you are interested, not interested, or need more information.

steps.action: **Check legitimacy.** Verify the recruiter's name, company, email domain, profile, and whether the role seems real.
steps.expect: obvious scams or impersonation are filtered out.

steps.action: **Decide your stance.** [BRANCH: interested | unsure | not interested] choose whether to pursue, ask questions, or decline.
steps.expect: the reply has a clear purpose.

steps.action: **Reply with the key signal.** For interest, write "I'm open to learning more"; for decline, write "I'm not looking right now."
steps.expect: the recruiter knows your position.

steps.action: **Ask for essentials if interested.** Request role scope, company, location or remote policy, compensation range, interview process, and visa or work authorization constraints if relevant.
steps.expect: you can screen fit before a call.

steps.action: **Offer availability.** Provide 2-3 time windows and timezone if you want a call.
steps.expect: scheduling can happen without back-and-forth.

steps.action: **Set boundaries.** Say what roles, locations, salary range, or timing you will consider.
steps.expect: future outreach is better targeted.

steps.action: **Protect sensitive information.** Do not send SSN, bank details, copies of ID, or confidential work samples during initial outreach.
steps.expect: your response shares only professional information.

steps.action: **Track the conversation.** Save the role, recruiter, date, and next step in a job-search tracker or notes.
steps.expect: you can follow up without confusion.

recipes.verification: Your reply clearly states interest level, asks for or provides the next step, protects sensitive information, and records the recruiter and role for follow-up.

recipes.title: run a brainstorming session
recipes.name: run-a-brainstorming-session
recipes.goal: Run a focused brainstorming session that produces usable options, not just a lively conversation.

steps.action: **Define the prompt.** Write a narrow question such as "How might we reduce onboarding time from 10 days to 5 without adding headcount?"
steps.expect: participants know the problem and constraint.

steps.action: **Invite the right mix.** Include people with user knowledge, delivery knowledge, and decision authority, but keep the group small enough to participate.
steps.expect: the room has useful perspectives without becoming a crowd.

steps.action: **Set constraints.** State time box, decision owner, budget limits, and what will happen after the session.
steps.expect: ideas are grounded in reality.

steps.action: **Generate silently first.** Give 5-10 minutes for individual idea writing before discussion.
steps.expect: quieter participants contribute before anchoring starts.

steps.action: **Share ideas round-robin.** Ask each person to add one idea at a time without debate.
steps.expect: ideas are captured before evaluation.

steps.action: **Cluster themes.** Group similar ideas and name each cluster in plain language.
steps.expect: the team can see patterns instead of a long raw list.

steps.action: **Select next experiments.** [BRANCH: vote | decision owner chooses] vote when input matters most; have the decision owner choose when accountability matters most.
steps.expect: the strongest options move forward.

steps.action: **Close with owners.** Assign an owner, next step, and decision date for each selected idea.
steps.expect: the brainstorm turns into action.

recipes.verification: The session ends with captured ideas, grouped themes, 2-5 selected options, named owners, and a date for deciding or testing next steps.

recipes.title: run a one on one meeting
recipes.name: run-a-one-on-one-meeting
recipes.goal: A one-on-one meeting gives the other person useful attention, surfaces issues early, and ends with clear actions.

steps.action: **Create a shared agenda.** Add a living document or note with sections for their topics, your topics, decisions, and actions.
steps.expect: both people can shape the meeting before it starts.

steps.action: **Invite their topics first.** Ask what they most want to cover and start there unless something urgent overrides it.
steps.expect: the meeting is not only your broadcast.

steps.action: **Separate status from substance.** Move simple updates to writing and use live time for blockers, decisions, feedback, growth, or relationship repair.
steps.expect: the conversation uses the value of being together.

steps.action: **Listen before solving.** Ask follow-up questions, reflect what you heard, and avoid jumping to advice before the problem is clear.
steps.expect: the other person feels understood and the real issue is visible.

steps.action: **Discuss feedback or support plainly.** [BRANCH: manager-led | peer-led] Managers should cover priorities, development, and support; peers should cover coordination, decisions, and friction.
steps.expect: the conversation matches the relationship.

steps.action: **Capture actions live.** Write owner, action, and date for each commitment while both people can correct it.
steps.expect: next steps are not hidden in memory.

steps.action: **Keep confidentiality boundaries.** ⚠️ *Irreversible:* sensitive personal or personnel information can spread through notes, so record only what belongs in a work system.
steps.expect: notes are useful without overexposing private details.

steps.action: **Protect the cadence.** End by confirming the next meeting and whether the frequency still works.
steps.expect: one-on-ones remain a reliable channel.

recipes.verification: The one-on-one used a shared agenda, covered the other person's topics first, captured action owners and dates, and confirmed the next cadence.

recipes.title: run a small meeting
recipes.name: run-a-small-meeting
recipes.goal: A meeting of roughly 3 to 8 people runs against a written agenda, every item reaches a recorded decision or a named owner, and it ends on time or early with a shared record of who does what next.

steps.action: **Send the agenda before the meeting, not during.** Paste it into the invite or a message the day before so people arrive prepared.
steps.expect: attendees can see the item list and the decision each item asks for.

steps.action: **Start on time with the goal, not with small talk.** State the purpose in one sentence and the hard stop.
steps.expect: the room quiets and orients; late arrivals catch up without a restart.

steps.action: **Assign a timekeeper and a note-taker.** For a small meeting you can hold both, but naming them out loud makes it real.
steps.expect: someone is watching the clock and someone is writing decisions down.

steps.action: **Walk items in order, one at a time.** Introduce the item, let the relevant people speak, then drive to a decision.
steps.expect: discussion stays on the current item; tangents get named and deferred.

steps.action: **When an item runs over its budget, force a fork.** [BRANCH: decide now with the information present | assign an owner to resolve it offline by a date | park it for a later meeting]
steps.expect: the clock is respected; nothing stalls the whole agenda.

steps.action: **Capture every decision as it happens, out loud.** Say "so the decision is X, owner is Y, by Z" and write it verbatim.
steps.expect: the owner hears their name and does not object; the note matches what was said.

steps.action: **Catch parking-lot items explicitly.** When something off-agenda but real comes up, write it in a visible "parking lot" and move on.
steps.expect: the raiser feels heard without the meeting derailing.

steps.action: **Close by reading back the decisions and owners.** Two minutes, out loud, before anyone leaves.
steps.expect: no one is surprised later; corrections happen now while everyone is present.

steps.action: **End early if the work is done.** Do not fill the booked time.
steps.expect: the meeting releases people ahead of the hard stop when possible.

steps.action: **Send the notes within a few hours.** Decisions, owners, dates, and the parking lot, in that order.
steps.expect: a written record reaches every attendee plus anyone who missed it.

recipes.verification: The meeting ended at or before its scheduled end, every agenda item has a recorded outcome (decision, owner with date, or explicit park), and a written summary listing decisions and owners was sent to all attendees.

recipes.title: schedule a meeting
recipes.name: schedule-a-meeting
recipes.goal: A meeting exists on every participant's calendar at a time they actually agreed to, with the purpose, location/link, and duration clear — and it happens.

steps.action: **Define the meeting in one line + a duration.** "30 min — decide the venue for the offsite." Purpose decides the invite list; duration defaults short (25/50 min beats 30/60 — buffer is humane).
steps.expect: a title anyone can parse, a duration you can defend.

steps.action: **Find candidate times against *their* constraints.** [BRANCH: same org → calendar's free/busy overlay, pick open slots | cross-org → offer 2–3 concrete windows by email, or send a scheduling link] Time zones: state times *in theirs* or use the tool's auto-conversion — never make a group do arithmetic.
steps.expect: 1–3 candidate slots that are genuinely open for the key people.

steps.action: **Send the invite with everything a participant needs.** Title (from step 1), the video link *or* room, agenda/one-liner in the description, any pre-reading attached or linked. Optional attendees marked optional.
steps.expect: invite lands on calendars pending acceptance; nothing crucial lives only in a separate email.

steps.action: **Watch the responses.** Accepts roll in → done. Key person declines/counter-proposes → take their counter-slot if it works: one renegotiation round maximum before you fall back to a scheduling poll.
steps.expect: all required participants accepted; the calendar object is the single source of truth.

steps.action: **Adjust by *updating the event*, never by side-channel agreement.** Time changes, link changes, room changes go through the calendar edit so every copy updates.
steps.expect: everyone's calendar shows the current truth; no "wait, I thought it moved" class of failure.

steps.action: **Day-of: honor it.** Join/arrive on time; if you must cancel, cancel the event (with a line of context) as early as known — a canceled meeting returns time, a no-show burns trust.
steps.expect: the meeting occurs at the stated time with the people it needed.

recipes.verification: Every required participant's calendar shows the same event — right time (their zone), working link/room, purpose readable — they accepted it, and the meeting subsequently happened (or was explicitly, promptly canceled).

recipes.title: send a package
recipes.name: send-a-package
recipes.goal: A parcel is packed to survive transit, correctly addressed and labeled, handed to a carrier with tracking, and it arrives.

steps.action: **Pack to the shake test.** Item centered with ~3 cm cushioning on all sides; fill voids until *nothing shifts when shaken*; heavy items in strong boxes, fragiles double-boxed if they matter.
steps.expect: a shaken box that sounds like a solid object, not maracas.

steps.action: **Seal with real packing tape.** H-pattern: along the center seam and across both edge seams, top and bottom. (Not household sticky tape, not string — string jams machinery.)
steps.expect: seams fully covered; flaps immobile.

steps.action: **Address it.** Recipient block (name, street, unit, city, postal code, country, phone) large and flat on the *top* face; your return address smaller, top-left or back. Remove/black out any old labels and barcodes on a reused box.
steps.expect: one unambiguous address block; zero stale barcodes.

steps.action: **Choose the service.** [BRANCH: post office (cheap, fine for non-urgent) | courier (faster, door pickup, better tracking) | drop-off point/locker networks (cheapest hybrid)] Compare on the two axes that matter: deadline and value. Insure above the carrier's default liability if the contents warrant.
steps.expect: service chosen with a known price, ETA, and insurance level.

steps.action: **Buy the label and declare honestly.** At the counter, kiosk, or online (online is usually cheaper — print or QR at drop-off). International: the customs form wants contents, value, and category truthfully — vague or false declarations park parcels in customs.
steps.expect: label affixed flat on the top face; customs form attached in its pouch if international.

steps.action: **Hand over and keep the proof.** Counter, pickup, or locker; take the receipt with the tracking number. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* once in the stream, contents are committed — the last look inside happens before step 2's tape.
steps.expect: receipt + tracking number saved; first scan appears within hours.

steps.action: **Send the tracking number to the recipient and watch delivery.** They can catch failed-delivery notices on their end.
steps.expect: tracking progresses to "delivered"; recipient confirms.

recipes.verification: The receipt's tracking number is saved and shared, tracking reached "delivered", and the recipient confirms contents arrived intact — or a documented claim/trace is in motion.

recipes.title: set an out of office reply
recipes.name: set-an-out-of-office-reply
recipes.goal: Set an automatic out-of-office reply that tells senders when to expect you back and who can help while you are unavailable.

steps.action: **Choose the date range.** Set the first unavailable day and the day replies should stop, including time zone if your tool asks.
steps.expect: the automatic reply has a scheduled start and end.

steps.action: **Write the core message.** State that you are away, when you return, and whether email will be monitored.
steps.expect: the sender can tell when a normal reply is likely.

steps.action: **Add an alternative contact.** Include a name, role, and email or phone only if that person has agreed to cover.
steps.expect: urgent senders have a valid path that will not surprise the contact.

steps.action: **Set the scope.** [BRANCH: internal only | external only | both] use internal details for coworkers and a shorter, safer message for outside senders.
steps.expect: sensitive internal information is not exposed to strangers.

steps.action: **Avoid oversharing.** Do not include home address, hotel, personal travel details, or a promise that the inbox is completely unmonitored unless necessary.
steps.expect: the message is useful without advertising too much absence.

steps.action: **Turn on calendar or chat status if needed.** Add an out-of-office calendar block or do-not-disturb status that matches the same dates.
steps.expect: meeting schedulers and chat users see your availability.

steps.action: **Send a test if possible.** Use another account or preview function to check formatting, links, signature, and dates.
steps.expect: the reply reads correctly on a normal received message.

steps.action: **Set a return reminder.** If the system does not auto-end, create a reminder to turn it off when you return.
steps.expect: you will not keep sending stale away messages.

recipes.verification: A test or preview shows the correct away dates, expected response timing, alternative contact, recipient scope, and automatic stop or reminder.

recipes.title: set up an email newsletter
recipes.name: set-up-an-email-newsletter
recipes.goal: Set up an email newsletter with a clear audience, consent-based list, sending cadence, content plan, and compliance checks.

steps.action: **Define the audience and promise.** Write who the newsletter is for and what useful information they will receive.
steps.expect: the newsletter has a reason to exist.

steps.action: **Choose the sending tool.** Use an approved platform that supports lists, templates, unsubscribe, sender identity, and analytics.
steps.expect: the tool can send responsibly.

steps.action: **Build the list lawfully.** [BRANCH: internal list | external list] use authorized employee groups for internal mail; use opt-in or permitted customer lists for external mail.
steps.expect: recipients are eligible to receive messages.

steps.action: **Create the template.** Add sender name, subject pattern, intro, sections, call to action, footer, and unsubscribe or preference link where required.
steps.expect: each issue has a consistent structure.

steps.action: **Plan the first four issues.** Draft topics, owners, send dates, and source links.
steps.expect: cadence is sustainable beyond the first send.

steps.action: **Test deliverability and display.** Send a test to yourself and a reviewer, checking links, mobile layout, images, spelling, and tracking.
steps.expect: mistakes are caught before launch.

steps.action: **Send the launch issue.** Send at the chosen time and monitor bounces, replies, unsubscribes, and errors.
steps.expect: the first issue reaches the intended list.

steps.action: **Review performance.** After 24-72 hours, record opens, clicks, replies, unsubscribes, and content feedback.
steps.expect: future issues can improve.

recipes.verification: The newsletter has an approved sending tool, eligible recipient list, reusable template, content calendar, tested launch issue, and recorded performance metrics.

recipes.title: take clear meeting minutes
recipes.name: take-clear-meeting-minutes
recipes.goal: Capture meeting minutes that preserve decisions, action items, owners, and useful context without becoming a transcript.

steps.action: **Create the note structure.** Set headings for attendees, decisions, action items, open questions, and context links.
steps.expect: notes are ready before discussion starts.

steps.action: **Record attendance.** List who attended, who was absent, and who represented each function if relevant.
steps.expect: readers know whose input was present.

steps.action: **Capture decisions as decisions.** Write "Decision: We will do X because Y; owner is Z."
steps.expect: decisions are not buried in discussion notes.

steps.action: **Track actions live.** For each action, write owner, deliverable, due date, and dependency.
steps.expect: follow-up work is assignable.

steps.action: **Summarize discussion selectively.** Include key tradeoffs, objections, and evidence, not every sentence.
steps.expect: absent stakeholders understand the reasoning.

steps.action: **Clarify ambiguous items.** Ask "Can I capture that as an action for Pat by Thursday?" when ownership is unclear.
steps.expect: the group confirms wording in real time.

steps.action: **Send minutes promptly.** [BRANCH: small team | formal meeting] send informal minutes in the team channel; send formal minutes by email or approved repository.
steps.expect: participants can correct mistakes while memory is fresh.

steps.action: **Update the source of truth.** Copy decisions and action items into the project tracker or decision log.
steps.expect: minutes drive execution beyond the meeting.

recipes.verification: The minutes identify attendees, decisions, action items with owners and dates, open questions, and a distribution location visible to the intended audience.

recipes.title: write a business proposal
recipes.name: write-a-business-proposal
recipes.goal: Write a business proposal that connects a customer or stakeholder problem to a credible solution, scope, timeline, price, and decision request.

steps.action: **Clarify the audience.** Identify the decision-maker, influencers, users, and procurement or finance reviewers.
steps.expect: the proposal speaks to the right concerns.

steps.action: **State the problem.** Write the current pain, impact, and cost of doing nothing.
steps.expect: the reader understands why action is needed.

steps.action: **Present the solution.** Describe what you will do, how it works, and why it fits the stated problem.
steps.expect: the proposal has a clear recommendation.

steps.action: **Define scope.** Include deliverables, exclusions, assumptions, timeline, dependencies, and acceptance criteria.
steps.expect: boundaries are explicit.

steps.action: **Show value and proof.** Add relevant metrics, case examples, qualifications, or expected return.
steps.expect: the reader can justify the investment.

steps.action: **Include price and terms.** [BRANCH: fixed fee | phased proposal] state one fixed price for clear scope; propose paid discovery or phases when uncertainty is high.
steps.expect: commercial terms match risk.

steps.action: **Name risks and mitigations.** Explain schedule, adoption, technical, legal, or resource risks and how they will be managed.
steps.expect: credibility increases because limits are visible.

steps.action: **Close with next step.** Ask for approval, signature, meeting, pilot, or procurement action by a specific date.
steps.expect: the reader knows how to proceed.

recipes.verification: The proposal includes problem, solution, scope, exclusions, timeline, price or commercial approach, proof, risks, and a specific decision request.

recipes.title: write a complaint letter
recipes.name: write-a-complaint-letter
recipes.goal: A complaint letter that states the facts, asks for a specific remedy, and creates a clear record without sounding careless or hostile.

steps.action: **Gather the record first.** Put dates, amounts, reference numbers, names, and evidence in one place.
steps.expect: the complaint rests on checkable facts.

steps.action: **Address the right office.** Use customer relations, landlord, school office, regulator, or manager as appropriate.
steps.expect: the letter reaches someone with authority to act.

steps.action: **Open with the issue and desired outcome.** State what happened and what you want in the first paragraph.
steps.expect: the reader knows the purpose immediately.

steps.action: **Lay out facts in order.** Use short paragraphs or bullets with dates, what was promised, what happened, and what you already tried.
steps.expect: the timeline is easy to follow.

steps.action: **Stay calm and firm.** Remove insults, sarcasm, threats you cannot follow through on, and broad claims you cannot prove.
steps.expect: the letter sounds credible under review.

steps.action: **Name the remedy and deadline.** [BRANCH: simple fix | formal escalation] Ask for the specific fix and a reasonable response date; if rights or money are involved, cite the policy or law you are relying on.
steps.expect: the recipient knows what action would resolve it.

steps.action: **Include the escalation path.** Say what you will do next if there is no response, such as contacting a regulator, card issuer, tenant board, or supervisor.
steps.expect: escalation is clear without sounding reckless.

steps.action: **Check before sending.** Attach evidence, save a copy, and verify the address. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* sending false claims or private information to the wrong party can cause real harm, so confirm every factual allegation.
steps.expect: the sent letter is accurate and preserved.

recipes.verification: The letter includes facts and dates, a specific remedy, a response deadline, evidence, escalation path, and a saved copy.

recipes.title: write a cover letter
recipes.name: write-a-cover-letter
recipes.goal: Write a concise cover letter that connects your experience to a specific role and is ready to submit with a job application.

steps.action: **Read the role for signals.** Highlight the job title, required skills, team mission, and repeated words.
steps.expect: a short list of 3 to 5 role priorities.

steps.action: **Choose the main match.** Pick the strongest reason you fit this role, not every reason you are qualified.
steps.expect: one sentence can explain why this application makes sense.

steps.action: **Open with the role and fit.** Name the position and state the relevant strength you bring.
steps.expect: first paragraph identifies the job and avoids generic filler.

steps.action: **Show, do not tell.** Use one concrete example with action, context, and result instead of claiming you are passionate or hardworking.
steps.expect: the reader can picture what you did.

steps.action: **Tie the example back to the employer.** Explain how that experience helps with the role's stated needs.
steps.expect: the letter feels tailored to this posting.

steps.action: **Keep the length controlled.** Aim for 250 to 400 words, usually 3 or 4 short paragraphs.
steps.expect: the letter fits on one page with readable spacing.

steps.action: **Close with next action.** Thank the reader and say you would welcome a conversation.
steps.expect: ending is polite and does not pressure the employer.

steps.action: **Proofread in layers.** Check names, job title, spelling, dates, and copied text from old letters.
steps.expect: no wrong company name, wrong role, or obvious typo remains.

steps.action: **Save in the requested format.** Export PDF unless the application asks for plain text or a document file.
steps.expect: filename and format are ready for upload.

recipes.verification: The final letter names the correct role and employer, includes one specific evidence-based example, stays under one page, and has been proofread against the posting.

recipes.title: write a formal email
recipes.name: write-a-formal-email
recipes.goal: A formal email — to an official, professor, landlord, HR, customer service, or a stranger with power over your outcome — that gets read, understood, and acted on, in one send.

steps.action: **Write the body before the To: field.** (Old professional armor: no premature sends.) Start from the ask, not the throat-clearing.
steps.expect: drafting happens with an empty recipient field.

steps.action: **Subject line = topic + specificity.** "Repair request — Flat 3B bathroom leak" beats "Question"; include reference numbers where they exist ("Application #48213").
steps.expect: a subject the recipient could file, forward, and find again.

steps.action: **Open with the right register and name.** "Dear Dr. Lee," / "Dear Sir or Madam," (unknown) / "Hello Support team,". When unsure of formality, err formal — recipients downgrade gracefully, upgrades read as correction.
steps.expect: a greeting matched to the relationship, names spelled right (check twice; it's the cheapest respect).

steps.action: **State who you are and what you want in the first two sentences.** "I'm the tenant at X. I'm writing to request Y." Context *after* the ask, not before — busy readers triage on sentence one.
steps.expect: a recipient who knows the ask before their first scroll.

steps.action: **Give the supporting facts in scannable form.** Short paragraphs or a compact list: dates, amounts, reference numbers, what you've already tried. Attach evidence and *name the attachments in the text* ("photos attached").
steps.expect: everything needed to act, nothing that pads; attachments actually attached (the classic — see F1).

steps.action: **Close with the explicit next step and a deadline where legitimate.** "Could you confirm the repair date by Friday the 25th?" — a formal email without a requested action invites a filed-and-forgotten. Then the sign-off: "Kind regards, / Full Name / contact."
steps.expect: the recipient knows exactly what doing-their-part looks like.

steps.action: **The pre-send pass.** Read once aloud-ish: tone (would you say this to their face?), typos, the name again, attachment present, recipient *now* added and correct. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* send is send — wrong-recipient and reply-all-with-heat are the two classic unrecoverables; this pass is where they die.
steps.expect: one clean send.

recipes.verification: One send contained: findable subject, correct name and register, the ask in sentence two, scannable facts, named-and-present attachments, an explicit requested action — and the thread now serves as its own paper trail (`housing/report-a-repair-to-your-landlord` step 3's principle, generalized).

recipes.title: write a job description
recipes.name: write-a-job-description
recipes.goal: Write a job description that accurately explains the role, attracts qualified candidates, and supports a fair hiring process.

steps.action: **Define the business need.** Write why the role exists and what problem the hire will solve in the next 6-12 months.
steps.expect: the description is anchored in real work.

steps.action: **List core responsibilities.** Include 5-8 recurring responsibilities and expected outcomes, not every possible task.
steps.expect: candidates can picture the job.

steps.action: **Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves.** Keep must-haves limited to skills truly needed on day one.
steps.expect: requirements do not screen out qualified candidates unnecessarily.

steps.action: **Describe success.** Add first-year outcomes such as "launch monthly reporting cadence" or "reduce ticket backlog by 30%."
steps.expect: performance expectations are concrete.

steps.action: **Use inclusive, plain language.** Remove jargon, inflated credentials, gender-coded wording, and unnecessary years of experience.
steps.expect: the posting is readable and fair.

steps.action: **Add logistics and range.** [BRANCH: remote | on-site] state timezone and travel expectations for remote roles; state location, schedule, and physical requirements for on-site roles.
steps.expect: candidates know constraints before applying.

steps.action: **Review for legal and policy fit.** Check equal opportunity language, pay transparency rules, and internal approval requirements.
steps.expect: the posting can be published responsibly.

steps.action: **Align the interview plan.** Map each requirement to an interview question, exercise, or evidence source.
steps.expect: hiring evaluates what the description promises.

recipes.verification: The job description includes role purpose, responsibilities, required qualifications, nice-to-haves, success outcomes, logistics, approved range or policy language, and an interview plan mapping.

recipes.title: write a linkedin connection note
recipes.name: write-a-linkedin-connection-note
recipes.goal: Write a LinkedIn connection note that gives the recipient a clear reason to accept, feels human, and does not immediately demand time, referrals, or favors.

steps.action: **Identify why this person.** Read their headline, recent work, shared groups, mutual contacts, or where you met.
steps.expect: one specific reason is available without pretending familiarity.

steps.action: **Choose the hook.** Use the most natural connection: "I enjoyed your panel," "We both worked with Sam," "Your post on clinical operations was useful."
steps.expect: the note could not be sent unchanged to 50 people.

steps.action: **Keep it short.** Aim for 2 or 3 sentences and about 250 characters if the interface limits notes.
steps.expect: the recipient can understand it in one glance.

steps.action: **Name why you, lightly.** Include your relevant role or context only if it helps: "I work on hospital analytics" or "I'm a recent alum exploring policy roles."
steps.expect: they know where you fit without reading your whole profile.

steps.action: **Avoid the immediate ask.** Do not request a referral, job, meeting, pitch review, or customer intro in the connection note. [BRANCH: met before | cold note] mention the meeting if you met; use admiration plus relevance if cold.
steps.expect: accepting does not feel like agreeing to work.

steps.action: **Write the final note.** Example: "Hi Maya, I appreciated your comments on patient intake at the HIMSS panel. I work on clinic workflow tools and would enjoy following your work here."
steps.expect: the note is specific, brief, and low-pressure.

steps.action: **Review tone before sending.** Remove flattery that sounds inflated, generic "synergy" language, and any false closeness. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* once sent, a connection note cannot usually be edited or unsent.
steps.expect: the final text is professional and true.

steps.action: **Send and wait.** If they accept, do not immediately pile on a large request; let the connection breathe or send a separate thoughtful follow-up later.
steps.expect: the relationship starts with context, not extraction.

recipes.verification: The note is under the platform limit, includes one specific hook, identifies your relevant context, and contains no immediate favor request.

recipes.title: write a networking follow up
recipes.name: write-a-networking-follow-up
recipes.goal: Write a networking follow-up that reminds the person who you are, preserves the relationship, and makes any ask easy to answer.

steps.action: **Follow up promptly.** Send the note within 24-48 hours while the interaction is still memorable.
steps.expect: the recipient can place you.

steps.action: **Use a clear subject.** Write a subject like "Great meeting you at the product analytics event" or "Thank you for the intro."
steps.expect: the message is recognizable.

steps.action: **Remind them of context.** Mention where you met and one specific topic you discussed.
steps.expect: the note does not feel generic.

steps.action: **Add useful value.** Share a promised link, article, contact, or concise reflection from the conversation.
steps.expect: the follow-up gives before it asks.

steps.action: **Make one ask if needed.** [BRANCH: thank-you only | specific ask] close warmly for thank-you only; ask one bounded question, introduction, or 20-minute chat for a specific ask.
steps.expect: the recipient can respond easily.

steps.action: **Keep it short.** Limit the note to a few short paragraphs and remove life story details.
steps.expect: the message is easy to read on mobile.

steps.action: **Offer an easy out.** Use "If now is not a good time, no worries" when asking for time or help.
steps.expect: the relationship stays low-pressure.

steps.action: **Set a reminder.** If you made an ask, note when to follow up once, usually after one week.
steps.expect: you do not accidentally pester them.

recipes.verification: The follow-up includes context, a specific reference, optional useful value, no more than one clear ask, and a respectful close.

recipes.title: write a project status update
recipes.name: write-a-project-status-update
recipes.goal: Write a project status update that gives stakeholders current state, risks, decisions needed, and next actions without requiring a meeting.

steps.action: **Start with a status line.** Write "Status: Green/Yellow/Red" plus one sentence explaining schedule, scope, and confidence.
steps.expect: readers know the project state immediately.

steps.action: **Summarize progress.** List the concrete work completed since the last update, using artifacts or metrics where possible.
steps.expect: stakeholders can see movement.

steps.action: **Name risks and blockers.** State each risk, impact, owner, and date when it must be resolved.
steps.expect: unresolved issues are visible early.

steps.action: **Call out decisions needed.** Use "Decision needed: approve X by Friday so Y can proceed."
steps.expect: decision-makers know exactly what action is required.

steps.action: **List next actions.** Include owner, action, and due date for each near-term task.
steps.expect: the update creates accountability.

steps.action: **Use consistent labels.** [BRANCH: internal update | client update] use internal project names for internal readers; translate jargon and remove internal blame for clients.
steps.expect: the update fits the audience.

steps.action: **Send to the right audience.** Share in the agreed channel and tag only people who need to act or stay informed.
steps.expect: stakeholders receive it without unnecessary noise.

steps.action: **Archive the update.** Link it from the project tracker or status doc.
steps.expect: future readers can find the update history.

recipes.verification: The update states green/yellow/red status, completed work, current risks, decisions requested, named next actions, and a date for the next update.

recipes.title: write a recommendation letter
recipes.name: write-a-recommendation-letter
recipes.goal: A recommendation letter that explains your relationship to the candidate, proves their strengths with specific examples, and helps the reader see the fit.

steps.action: **Confirm the ask and deadline.** Ask what the letter is for, where it goes, and when it is due.
steps.expect: the logistics are clear before you draft.

steps.action: **Define your relationship.** Open with who you are, how long you have known the candidate, and in what capacity.
steps.expect: the reader understands your basis for judgment.

steps.action: **Choose two or three strengths.** Pick qualities relevant to the opportunity, such as research judgment, leadership, care, reliability, or writing.
steps.expect: the letter has a focused argument.

steps.action: **Use specific examples.** Give concrete projects, moments, numbers, or behavior that show the qualities in action.
steps.expect: praise is supported rather than generic.

steps.action: **Explain the fit.** Connect the candidate's strengths to the role, program, lab, scholarship, or team they want to join.
steps.expect: the reader sees why this person belongs there.

steps.action: **Close strongly.** State your recommendation plainly and offer to be contacted for more information.
steps.expect: the final paragraph leaves no doubt about your support.

steps.action: **Check constraints before sending.** [BRANCH: confidential upload | candidate-visible letter] Upload directly if confidentiality is required; share a copy only if the process allows it. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* a submitted confidential letter usually cannot be edited or shown later, so verify names, dates, and recipient before submission.
steps.expect: the letter is sent through the correct channel.

steps.action: **Keep a dated copy.** Save the final version with the candidate's name and opportunity.
steps.expect: you can reuse accurate facts if asked again.

recipes.verification: The submitted letter states your relationship, gives specific examples, explains fit, closes with clear support, and includes your contact information if appropriate.

recipes.title: write a resignation letter
recipes.name: write-a-resignation-letter
recipes.goal: Write a short, professional resignation letter that states the resignation, final working date, notice period, thanks, and transition intent.

steps.action: **Confirm notice requirements.** Check contract, handbook, union agreement, or local law before drafting.
steps.expect: the minimum notice period is known.

steps.action: **Open with the decision.** State clearly that you are resigning from your position.
steps.expect: the first paragraph cannot be mistaken for a complaint or negotiation.

steps.action: **State the final date.** Include the calendar date of your last working day.
steps.expect: HR can calculate the notice period without guessing.

steps.action: **Keep reasons brief or omit them.** If you include a reason, make it neutral and factual.
steps.expect: the letter does not burn bridges.

steps.action: **Add thanks.** Mention appreciation for the opportunity, team, or experience in one sentence.
steps.expect: the tone remains professional even if circumstances are mixed.

steps.action: **Offer transition help.** Say you will help document work or hand over responsibilities during the notice period.
steps.expect: the employer knows you intend an orderly exit.

steps.action: **Review for risky language.** Remove blame, threats, jokes, or confidential details.
steps.expect: the letter would still look appropriate if forwarded to HR.

steps.action: **Send through the right channel.** [BRANCH: email | printed letter | HR portal] deliver it according to company practice after telling your manager if appropriate. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* submitting resignation may trigger offboarding, so confirm final date and decision before sending.
steps.expect: the manager or HR receives the resignation.

steps.action: **Save proof.** Keep a copy and any acknowledgement.
steps.expect: you can prove date, wording, and delivery.

recipes.verification: The letter states resignation, position, final working date, notice period compliance, thanks, and transition intent in a professional record you saved.

recipes.title: write a self review
recipes.name: write-a-self-review
recipes.goal: Write a self-review that gives your manager concrete evidence of impact, names growth honestly, and aligns your work to the goals you were supposed to advance.

steps.action: **Collect evidence before writing.** Pull calendar milestones, tickets, docs, dashboards, customer notes, peer feedback, and goal updates.
steps.expect: you have facts instead of memory fragments.

steps.action: **Map accomplishments to goals.** For each goal, state what you did, why it mattered, and what changed because of it.
steps.expect: the review follows business or team priorities, not only busyness.

steps.action: **Use impact and metrics.** Include numbers where honest: revenue, cycle time, defect rate, adoption, saved hours, risk reduced, users helped, launches completed.
steps.expect: claims are checkable.

steps.action: **Name your role clearly.** Say whether you led, owned, contributed, unblocked, reviewed, coordinated, or supported. Avoid taking credit for others and avoid disappearing your own work.
steps.expect: your actual contribution is visible.

steps.action: **Avoid the modesty trap.** Replace "just helped with" with precise verbs and outcomes. [BRANCH: individual contributor | manager] ICs emphasize shipped work and influence; managers include team outcomes, coaching, hiring, and operating rhythm.
steps.expect: the review is confident without being inflated.

steps.action: **Write growth areas with ownership.** Pick one or two real areas, describe what you learned, and state the next behavior: "I need to escalate dependency risk earlier, so I am adding weekly owner check-ins."
steps.expect: growth reads as maturity, not self-sabotage.

steps.action: **Connect to next goals.** Mention where you want to deepen scope, skills, leadership, quality, or customer impact next cycle.
steps.expect: the review gives your manager material for future planning.

steps.action: **Revise for evidence and tone.** Remove vague adjectives, defensiveness, and surprises. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* once submitted, the review may become part of your performance record, so verify dates, claims, and sensitive details.
steps.expect: every major statement has evidence and fits the rubric.

recipes.verification: The self-review ties accomplishments to goals, includes concrete impact or metrics, names growth areas with next actions, and matches the review rubric.

recipes.title: write a thank you note
recipes.name: write-a-thank-you-note
recipes.goal: You write and send a thank-you note that names a specific gift or act, expresses genuine appreciation, and reaches the recipient promptly.

steps.action: **Recall one specific detail.** Not "the gift" but "the blue scarf" or "driving me to the airport at 5 a.m." Specificity is what separates a real note from a form letter.
steps.expect: one concrete detail written on scratch paper.

steps.action: **Send it promptly.** Aim within a few days of a gift or favor, within two weeks of a wedding or interview. Late is still worth doing; a late note beats none.
steps.expect: a target send date set, sooner rather than later.

steps.action: **Open by naming the person and the thing.** "Dear [name], thank you so much for the [specific thing]."
steps.expect: the first sentence names both the person and the specific gift/act.

steps.action: **Add the second sentence: its impact.** Say how you used it, felt about it, or will use it. This is the sentence that proves you mean it.
steps.expect: a concrete statement of effect ("it kept me warm all week", "your advice changed how I prepared").

steps.action: **Close with warmth and a forward look.** "It was so thoughtful of you. I hope to see you soon." Then sign off.
steps.expect: three sentences total is plenty; you do not owe them a page.

steps.action: **Prefer handwriting when it carries weight.** For gifts, condolences, weddings, and mentors, handwritten on paper signals effort that email cannot.
steps.expect: the medium matches the occasion (handwritten for weighty thanks, email acceptable for casual/work-fast contexts).

steps.action: **Address, stamp, and send.** Double-check the spelling of the name and the address.
steps.expect: note sealed, correctly addressed, and in the mailbox (or sent).

recipes.verification: The note names the specific gift or act, states its impact in your own words, closes warmly, and is on its way to the correct address, ideally within the occasion's expected window.

recipes.title: back into a parking space
recipes.name: back-into-a-parking-space
recipes.goal: You reverse into a parking space slowly and accurately so leaving later is safer and forward-facing.

steps.action: **Choose a suitable space.** Prefer a space with clear lines, no pedestrians nearby, and enough room to swing the front of the car.
steps.expect: the space can be entered without rushing.

steps.action: **Signal and position wide.** Signal toward the space, pass it slightly, and angle or swing wide enough that the rear can turn in.
steps.expect: drivers behind understand you are parking.

steps.action: **Stop before reversing.** Check mirrors, camera, over-shoulder views, and both sides for pedestrians, carts, and moving cars.
steps.expect: the rear path is clear.

steps.action: **Reverse slowly toward the reference point.** [BRANCH: space on right | space on left] turn the wheel toward the space when your rear bumper or mirror lines up with the near parking line or adjacent car corner.
steps.expect: the rear of the car starts entering the space.

steps.action: **Use mirrors to track both lines.** Keep the vehicle centered between the painted lines and watch the front corners swing.
steps.expect: clearance remains on both sides.

steps.action: **Straighten as the car aligns.** Unwind the steering wheel when the car becomes parallel with the parking lines, then continue back slowly.
steps.expect: the vehicle moves straight into the space.

steps.action: **Stop before the curb, wall, or car behind.** Use mirrors, camera guidelines, parking sensors, and direct vision, but do not trust any one aid alone.
steps.expect: the car is fully inside the space without touching anything.

steps.action: **Settle the car.** Shift to park, set the parking brake if appropriate, and check that doors can open within the lines.
steps.expect: the vehicle is centered and ready to pull forward later.

recipes.verification: The vehicle is fully within the parking lines, centered enough for doors to open, clear of obstacles, and positioned to exit forward.

recipes.title: buy a local sim card
recipes.name: buy-a-local-sim-card
recipes.goal: Your phone has working local calls and mobile data on a local prepaid SIM, and you know how to top it up before the credit or validity runs out.

steps.action: **Confirm the unlock before leaving home.** Insert any other carrier's SIM; if the phone asks for an unlock code or shows "SIM not supported", request an unlock from your carrier now. Unlocks can take days to process.
steps.expect: a foreign SIM registers on a network, or your carrier confirms the unlock in writing.

steps.action: **Choose where to buy: official carrier store over airport kiosk.** [BRANCH: need connectivity the second you land → airport kiosk, accept the 2-3x markup | can wait an hour → official carrier store in town for fair pricing and proper registration]
steps.expect: a store selected; for kiosks, verify it sells an official carrier product, not a reseller SIM registered to a stranger.

steps.action: **Pick a prepaid tourist or data plan.** State your stay length and data needs; ask what happens after the bundle is consumed (hard stop vs. expensive per-MB billing) and the plan's validity period.
steps.expect: plan chosen with known price, data cap, validity days, and post-cap behavior.

steps.action: **Complete ID registration at the counter.** Hand over your passport; staff photograph or scan it and register the SIM to you. A SIM not registered to your own ID can be deactivated without notice in many countries.
steps.expect: registration done under your name; passport handed back; keep the SIM packaging, which carries the number and PUK code.

steps.action: **Have the SIM installed and activated before leaving the counter.** Ask the staff to insert it, enter any default PIN, and confirm activation. Store your home SIM in the packaging slot or a labeled pocket; it is tiny and easily lost.
steps.expect: signal bars with the local carrier's name on screen; home SIM stored safely.

steps.action: **Test calls and data on the spot.** Make a test call; load a non-cached website on mobile data with Wi-Fi off. [BRANCH: data fails but calls work → APN needs manual setup, step 7 | both work → step 8]
