recipes.verification: The act was named, the impact acknowledged, no defense rode along, repair was offered or asked about, one credible change was stated, and the other person's response was left entirely theirs. The long-run verification is the only one that counts: the behavior changed.

recipes.title: ask for a favor
recipes.name: ask-for-a-favor
recipes.goal: You have asked someone for a specific favor in a way that made yes easy and no comfortable, and afterward you closed the loop so they'd gladly say yes again.

steps.action: **Define the exact ask first.** Write the one sentence: what, when, how long it will take them, and the deadline. Vague asks get vague maybes.
steps.expect: a single sentence a stranger could act on, with an honest time estimate.

steps.action: **Pick the channel by size.** [BRANCH: small favor (minutes of their time) → text message, which lets them answer on their own clock | larger favor (hours, money-adjacent, or emotionally loaded) → ask in person or by call, then follow up with details in writing]
steps.expect: channel matched to size; big asks never arrive as a wall of text out of nowhere.

steps.action: **Ask directly, with minimal preamble.** One line of context, then the ask. Skip the long apology-ramp ("I hate to ask, I know you're so busy, I feel terrible...") which forces them to manage your feelings before they can even hear the request. Avoid the contentless "can I ask you a favor?" opener; it extracts a blind yes and people resent it.
steps.expect: your ask was fully stated within the first two sentences.

steps.action: **Give an explicit easy out.** Say the actual words: "and honestly, no worries at all if you can't, I have a backup." An escape hatch stated by you is worth ten implied ones; it converts pressured yeses into real ones.
steps.expect: the out is in the same message as the ask, and you genuinely have (or will find) the backup you claimed.

steps.action: **Make the yes cheap to execute.** Bundle everything they need: the address, the file, the dates, the login already shared, the form pre-filled. Every question they'd have to ask you is a tax on their yes.
steps.expect: they can complete the favor without a single clarifying question.

steps.action: **Accept the answer at face value.** Yes: thank them once, confirm logistics, stop selling. No or hesitation: "totally fine, thanks for considering it," and mean it; do not negotiate a no. A no gracefully received keeps the relationship fully intact for the next ask.
steps.expect: no repeated asking; hesitation was treated as a no.

steps.action: **Thank them promptly after the favor happens.** Same day, proportional to size: a warm text for small favors, something tangible (meal, small gift, conspicuous public credit) for large ones.
steps.expect: thanks delivered within 24 hours of the favor.

steps.action: **Close the loop with a report.** Tell them how it turned out: "made the flight with 20 minutes to spare," "the intro you made turned into an interview." The report is the underused half of gratitude; it shows the favor mattered and is the single best predictor they'll say yes next time.
steps.expect: they know the outcome of what they helped with, not just that you were grateful.

recipes.verification: The ask was one specific sentence with a stated easy out, the answer (either way) was accepted without pressure, and, if they did it: thanks landed within a day and they later heard the outcome. Test of success: you could comfortably ask this person for something again, and they'd be glad to hear from you.

recipes.title: ask for help in a store
recipes.name: ask-for-help-in-a-store
recipes.goal: You get the help you need in a store — finding an item, checking stock, or understanding a product — quickly and pleasantly for both sides.

steps.action: **Identify actual staff.** Uniform, name badge, lanyard, or behind a counter; restocking carts are a giveaway.
steps.expect: a person who works here, not a fellow shopper in an unlucky shirt (if wrong: everyone laughs, see F1).

steps.action: **Open with a polite interrupt at a good moment.** Wait for a pause if they're mid-customer; then: "Excuse me — could you help me find something?"
steps.expect: attention turned to you; nobody's transaction was trampled.

steps.action: **State the need concretely.** Name + use beats vague category: "AAA batteries" beats "batteries stuff"; unknown name → describe the job: "the sticky strips for hanging posters without nails." Show a phone photo if you have one.
steps.expect: recognition, or a clarifying question you can answer.

steps.action: **Accept the help in the form offered.** [BRANCH: verbal aisle pointer → repeat it back ("aisle 7, by the tape — thanks") | they walk you there → follow and let them lead | they check the system → wait]
steps.expect: you end up at the item or at a definitive answer.

steps.action: **Handle "not stocked" usefully.** Ask the two follow-ups that staff can actually answer: "Will it come back / can you order it?" and "Who nearby would carry it?"
steps.expect: a next action, not just a dead end.

steps.action: **Close with thanks.** Brief and genuine; if they went notably out of their way, say so.
steps.expect: interaction ends warm; you're a pleasant memory, which matters in stores you frequent.

recipes.verification: You hold the item or a definitive answer (out of stock + next action), the interaction cost the staff member under a minute of friction, and it ended with thanks.

recipes.title: ask someone on a date
recipes.name: ask-someone-on-a-date
recipes.goal: Ask someone on a date clearly and respectfully, with low pressure and full room for any answer.

steps.action: **Choose timing that leaves an exit.** Ask when they are not trapped at work, in a car, at your home, or under public pressure.
steps.expect: they can answer freely.

steps.action: **Be warm and brief.** Start with a simple personal note, not a confession monologue.
steps.expect: the ask feels human, not heavy.

steps.action: **Use the word date if clarity helps.** Say, "Would you like to get coffee with me as a date?"
steps.expect: the invitation is not hidden as vague hanging out.

steps.action: **Suggest something specific.** [BRANCH: in person | text] Offer a simple plan, such as coffee Saturday afternoon or a walk after work.
steps.expect: they know what yes would mean.

steps.action: **Keep pressure low.** Add "No pressure if not" only once, then stop.
steps.expect: the invitation gives space without begging.

steps.action: **Wait for the answer.** Do not fill silence with persuasion.
steps.expect: they have time to respond honestly.

steps.action: **Accept the answer cleanly.** If yes, make the plan; if no, say thanks for being direct and move on. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* do not ask in a way that could damage someone's job, housing, safety, or public dignity.
steps.expect: their answer is treated as final.

steps.action: **Behave normally afterward.** Do not punish, tease, or recruit friends to interpret the answer.
steps.expect: respect continues after the ask.

recipes.verification: You made one clear, specific, low-pressure invitation and accepted the response without persuasion, punishment, or repeated follow-up.

recipes.title: be a good houseguest
recipes.name: be-a-good-houseguest
recipes.goal: You stay in someone else's home while reducing work for the host and leaving the relationship better than you found it.

steps.action: **Confirm the plan.** Recheck dates, arrival time, parking, pets, and house rules before traveling.
steps.expect: the host knows exactly when to expect you.

steps.action: **Bring something useful.** Bring a small gift, groceries, coffee, flowers, or a treat suited to the household.
steps.expect: the item adds pleasure without creating work.

steps.action: **Arrive prepared.** Pack toiletries, chargers, medication, sleepwear, and any special dietary items.
steps.expect: you do not need emergency errands from the host.

steps.action: **Respect the schedule.** Ask about wake times, meals, work hours, and bathroom timing.
steps.expect: your routine fits around theirs.

steps.action: **Keep your area tidy.** Make the bed, contain luggage, and keep bathroom items together.
steps.expect: shared rooms remain usable.

steps.action: **Help without taking over.** [BRANCH: host welcomes help | host declines help] wash dishes or set the table, or step aside gracefully.
steps.expect: help reduces effort, not control.

steps.action: **Clean before leaving.** Strip sheets if asked, gather towels, remove trash, and check for belongings.
steps.expect: the room is easy to reset.

steps.action: **Send thanks.** Text the same day and follow with a note or small gesture for a longer stay.
steps.expect: the host feels appreciated after you leave.

recipes.verification: At departure, your sleeping area and shared spaces are tidy, the host knows you are grateful, and no unresolved mess or damage is hidden.

recipes.title: be a good listener
recipes.name: be-a-good-listener
recipes.goal: Help another person feel heard without taking over the conversation.

steps.action: **Put attention where they can see it.** Face the person, put the phone away, and stop side tasks.
steps.expect: your body and eyes show that the conversation has priority.

steps.action: **Invite the topic without steering it.** Ask "What happened?" or "What do you want me to understand?"
steps.expect: they choose the starting point.

steps.action: **Let the first pass run.** Do not interrupt the first full explanation unless you cannot hear or understand.
steps.expect: they finish a thought without having to defend the floor.

steps.action: **Reflect back the core.** Say the short version of what you heard, including the feeling if clear.
steps.expect: they can confirm, correct, or sharpen it.

steps.action: **Ask questions before advice.** Use open questions such as "What part is bothering you most?" or "What have you tried?"
steps.expect: the next answer gives more detail instead of shutting down.

steps.action: **Check before fixing.** [BRANCH: they want advice | they want listening] ask "Do you want ideas, or do you want me to just listen?"
steps.expect: the role is explicit.

steps.action: **Use silence without panic.** Wait a few seconds after an emotional sentence instead of filling the gap.
steps.expect: they either continue or visibly settle.

steps.action: **Name limits gently.** If time is short, say how much time you have and offer a later continuation.
steps.expect: the conversation has a clear boundary without abruptness.

steps.action: **Close by summarizing support.** Mention one thing you understood and one next action only if they named it.
steps.expect: they leave knowing what you heard, not what you imposed.

recipes.verification: The other person has spoken more than you, has corrected or confirmed your summary, and knows whether you are listening or advising.

recipes.title: be a good plus one
recipes.name: be-a-good-plus-one
recipes.goal: Attend an event as someone's guest in a way that supports your host, respects the occasion, and leaves people glad you came.

steps.action: **Get briefed before arrival.** Ask your host for names to know, relationships, dress code, gift expectations, and any tensions.
steps.expect: you can recognize a few key people and avoid obvious mistakes.

steps.action: **Arrive as a unit.** Be on time, dressed appropriately, and ready to follow your host's lead for greetings, seating, and introductions.
steps.expect: your host does not have to manage your lateness or confusion.

steps.action: **Learn a few names.** Repeat names once, connect them to context, and use them when saying goodbye.
steps.expect: at least three people feel noticed instead of treated as background.

steps.action: **Help your host lightly.** Offer to hold a bag, get water, make conversation with someone, take a photo, or rescue them from a stuck conversation. [BRANCH: social event | work event] be warmer and looser at social events; be more restrained at work events.
steps.expect: your presence makes the night easier for the person who brought you.

steps.action: **Do not disappear.** Step away for bathroom, calls, or conversation, but tell your host if you will be gone more than a few minutes.
steps.expect: your host never has to search the room anxiously.

steps.action: **Do not overdrink or overperform.** Keep alcohol and jokes below the level where your host becomes responsible for you.
steps.expect: you remain steady, readable, and appropriate to the room.

steps.action: **Respect photos and private context.** Ask before posting, especially at weddings, work events, launches, or family gatherings. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* public posts can reveal attendance, relationships, or news before hosts are ready.
steps.expect: no one has to ask you to remove a photo.

steps.action: **Thank the host and your inviter.** Say goodbye to the event host when practical, then thank the person who invited you on the way home or the next day.
steps.expect: both hosts know you appreciated being included.

recipes.verification: You arrived prepared, supported your host, stayed appropriate, remained findable, and thanked both your inviter and the event host when possible.

recipes.title: be a good wedding guest
recipes.name: be-a-good-wedding-guest
recipes.goal: You attend a wedding in a way that respects the couple, the schedule, the dress code, and the tone of the event.

steps.action: **RSVP on time.** Reply by the requested method before the deadline.
steps.expect: the couple or planner has your attendance count.

steps.action: **Follow the invite details.** Bring only named guests and respect adult-only or no-plus-one wording.
steps.expect: your plan matches the invitation.

steps.action: **Choose dress code first.** Read the stated dress code and venue clues before shopping or packing.
steps.expect: your outfit fits the level of formality.

steps.action: **Use the registry.** Buy from the registry or give money if that is customary for the couple.
steps.expect: the gift is useful and not a duplicate burden.

steps.action: **Arrive early.** Plan to be seated 10 to 15 minutes before the ceremony.
steps.expect: you are not entering during the processional.

steps.action: **Put the phone away.** Silence it and avoid aisle photos unless invited to take them.
steps.expect: the photographer and guests have clear views.

steps.action: **Respect reception timing.** Wait for meal, toast, dance, and exit cues from hosts or staff.
steps.expect: you do not interrupt planned moments.

steps.action: **Leave graciously.** Thank the couple or close family if practical, then depart without creating cleanup work.
steps.expect: your exit is calm and noticed only appropriately.

recipes.verification: You RSVP as requested, arrive before the ceremony starts, follow the dress code, and avoid disrupting ceremony, photos, meal, or toasts.

recipes.title: be a supportive friend
recipes.name: be-a-supportive-friend
recipes.goal: Support a friend through ordinary stress or difficulty by showing up, listening well, offering practical help, and following through.

steps.action: **Show up promptly.** Send a message, call, visit, or make plans based on what fits the relationship.
steps.expect: they know you noticed and care.

steps.action: **Ask what kind of support they want.** [BRANCH: listening | advice | practical help | distraction] Let them choose if they can.
steps.expect: you are not guessing loudly.

steps.action: **Listen more than you advise.** Reflect what you heard and ask one gentle question.
steps.expect: they feel accompanied, not managed.

steps.action: **Validate without taking over.** Say the situation sounds hard or unfair without making yourself the main character.
steps.expect: their experience stays central.

steps.action: **Offer practical help specifically.** Suggest food, rides, childcare, proofreading, errands, or sitting with them.
steps.expect: help is easy to accept or decline.

steps.action: **Do what you said.** Put reminders on your calendar for promised calls, meals, or check-ins. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* do not share their private situation with others unless they ask or safety requires it.
steps.expect: support becomes reliable action.

steps.action: **Remember the follow-up.** Check in after the appointment, anniversary, interview, funeral, or hard date.
steps.expect: they are not dropped after the first conversation.

steps.action: **Stay consistent within your limits.** Be honest about what you can do and keep showing up in small ways.
steps.expect: care is sustainable.

recipes.verification: Your friend received timely contact, was listened to before advice, got a specific offer of help, and had at least one remembered follow-up.

recipes.title: borrow and return an item
recipes.name: borrow-and-return-an-item
recipes.goal: An item is borrowed from a neighbor, friend, or colleague and returned in equal-or-better condition, on time — leaving the lending relationship stronger, not spent.

steps.action: **Ask with an easy out and a defined term.** "Any chance I could borrow your drill for an hour this afternoon? Totally fine if not." The escape hatch and the timeframe are what make it a small ask.
steps.expect: a genuine yes (or a no you accept gracefully at zero cost to either side).

steps.action: **Receive it with a condition glance.** Note the state together, casually: "Great — battery's about half, cool." Not an inspection ritual; one shared sentence that prevents later ambiguity.
steps.expect: both parties hold the same picture of the item's condition and accessories (case, bits, charger).

steps.action: **Use it within the asked scope.** The borrowed drill hangs one shelf; it does not renovate the bathroom or get sub-lent to your cousin. Scope creep is a new ask — make it explicitly if needed.
steps.expect: usage matches what was described.

steps.action: **Return it better than borrowed, on or before the term.** Charged, cleaned, refilled (fuel, tape, sugar replaced with a fresh bag), accessories complete. ⚠️ *Irreversible-ish:* late unprompted returns quietly re-price every future ask — the *lender having to ask for it back* is the relationship failure, not damage.
steps.expect: item back in their hands by the stated time, in better shape than it left.

steps.action: **Close with thanks + the report.** "Lifesaver — worked perfectly, I topped up the charge." Small reciprocity where natural (the beer, the returned favor, your own stuff lent freely).
steps.expect: the lender ends *gladder* they lent it; the channel stays open both ways.

recipes.verification: The item is back with its owner on time, complete and equal-or-better, they learned about any incident from you first, and the honest test: they'd say yes faster next time.

recipes.title: break bad news
recipes.name: break-bad-news
recipes.goal: Tell someone difficult news clearly, kindly, and privately while giving them room to react.

steps.action: **Prepare the core sentence.** Write one plain sentence that says what happened without euphemism.
steps.expect: you can say the news in under 20 seconds.

steps.action: **Choose the setting.** Use a private room, quiet call, or direct message only when live conversation is not possible.
steps.expect: the person will not be exposed in front of an audience.

steps.action: **Check availability.** Ask whether they can talk for a few minutes about something serious.
steps.expect: they either make space now or name a better near-term time.

steps.action: **Give a brief warning.** Say that you have bad news and will be direct.
steps.expect: their attention shifts before the main sentence.

steps.action: **Say the news plainly.** Deliver the prepared sentence without overexplaining first.
steps.expect: the key fact is unmistakable.

steps.action: **Let it land.** Stop talking for several seconds, and tolerate silence, tears, anger, or confusion.
steps.expect: they have room to process before details arrive.

steps.action: **Answer only what you know.** Share confirmed details and say "I do not know yet" when needed.
steps.expect: the conversation stays honest instead of padded with guesses.

steps.action: **Offer support.** Ask what they need now, and offer one concrete help option if appropriate.
steps.expect: they know they are not being abandoned with the news.

steps.action: **Close with next contact.** Agree on the next update, call, ride, meal, or person to notify.
steps.expect: there is a small next step after the first shock.

recipes.verification: The person has heard the main fact, has had time to react, and knows at least one concrete next step or support option.

recipes.title: break the ice in a group
recipes.name: break-the-ice-in-a-group
recipes.goal: A group that feels stiff or unfamiliar gets a light opening, shared ground, and a few people talking comfortably.

steps.action: **Use a light opener.** Comment on the shared setting, food, weather, event, or timing without complaining hard.
steps.expect: people can respond without revealing anything personal.

steps.action: **Ask an easy question.** Try "How do you know the host," "What brought you here," or "What has been the best part so far?"
steps.expect: one person has a simple answer ready.

steps.action: **Offer your own short answer.** Give enough of yourself to make the exchange balanced, then stop.
steps.expect: the conversation feels like sharing, not interviewing.

steps.action: **Find common ground.** Listen for overlaps in neighborhoods, work, hobbies, travel, kids, classes, or mutual friends.
steps.expect: the next question grows naturally from something said.

steps.action: **Bring others in.** [BRANCH: one quiet person | whole circle] Ask a nearby quiet person a low-pressure version, or turn the topic to the whole group if energy rises.
steps.expect: the conversation spreads beyond two people.

steps.action: **Keep topics gentle at first.** Avoid money, politics, health, dating history, religion, workplace gossip, and trauma until trust exists. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* an intrusive first question can mark you as unsafe, so stay easy before going deep.
steps.expect: nobody has to defend a boundary in minute one.

steps.action: **Hand off the conversation.** Connect two people who share an interest, then let them talk without controlling it.
steps.expect: the ice stays broken after you step back.

steps.action: **Exit gracefully if needed.** Say "I'm going to grab a drink, nice talking with you" when the exchange has run its course.
steps.expect: the end feels normal, not like rejection.

recipes.verification: At least two people have exchanged names or context, one shared topic is active, and no one was pressured into personal disclosure.

recipes.title: cancel plans gracefully
recipes.name: cancel-plans-gracefully
recipes.goal: Plans are canceled early, clearly, and kindly, with the other person left informed instead of stranded or guessing.

steps.action: **Decide promptly.** As soon as you know you cannot go, stop hoping the conflict will fix itself.
steps.expect: the other person gets the maximum possible notice.

steps.action: **Choose the direct channel.** [BRANCH: close or time-sensitive plan | casual low-stakes plan] call or text directly, or send a short message in the original thread.
steps.expect: the message reaches the person who needs to adjust.

steps.action: **State the cancellation first.** Say you cannot make it, naming the plan and date.
steps.expect: the main fact is clear in the first sentence.

steps.action: **Give a brief honest reason.** Use one sentence, such as illness, work conflict, family issue, low energy, or a scheduling mistake.
steps.expect: the reason is understandable without inviting debate.

steps.action: **Apologize once and take responsibility.** Say "I'm sorry for the late change" or "I'm sorry to miss it" without spiraling.
steps.expect: regret is expressed without making them manage your guilt.

steps.action: **Offer repair if needed.** [BRANCH: you want to reschedule | you do not] suggest two replacement windows, or simply wish them a good time.
steps.expect: the next step is easy to accept or decline.

steps.action: **Handle costs and logistics.** Transfer tickets, pay your share, release a reservation seat, or help find a replacement if appropriate. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* canceling a paid booking may trigger fees, so check the policy before pressing cancel.
steps.expect: your cancellation does not create avoidable work or cost for others.

steps.action: **Stop over-explaining.** After they respond, acknowledge once and move on.
steps.expect: the interaction ends cleanly and respectfully.

recipes.verification: The other person has received a clear cancellation before the event time, and any reservation, money, ticket, or reschedule issue has an explicit next step.

recipes.title: comfort someone
recipes.name: comfort-someone
recipes.goal: Someone in distress (bad news, a loss, a hard day) feels less alone after your presence, because you offered attention and warmth without trying to fix, minimize, or redirect their feelings.

steps.action: **Show up and open gently.** "Hey — I heard. I'm so sorry." or "You seem really down. Want company?" The offer includes a live exit for them.
steps.expect: an invitation in, or a "not now" that you honor gracefully (honoring it *is* comfort).

steps.action: **Let them talk, and listen without steering.** Attention on them, phone away, nods and small acknowledgments ("that's so hard", "of course you're upset"). Silence is allowed; they fill it when ready.
steps.expect: them doing most of the talking, at their pace, including quiet stretches you do not rush to fill.

steps.action: **Validate before anything else.** Their feeling is legitimate by definition; say so plainly: "Anyone would be gutted." Strike the minimizers from your vocabulary for this hour: "at least...", "everything happens for a reason", "others have it worse", "you'll be fine".
steps.expect: zero sentences that begin with "at least".

steps.action: **Resist the fix, unless asked.** Advice arrives only through the door they open ("what do you think I should do?"), and even then lightly. Uninvited solutions convert their grief into your project.
steps.expect: your suggestions held; if the urge wins, at most: "Do you want thoughts, or do you want me to just listen?" — the question itself is excellent comfort.

steps.action: **Offer concrete, small help instead of "let me know if you need anything".** The open offer transfers work to them; the specific one does the work: "I'm dropping dinner off tomorrow — any allergies?", "I'll take the airport run", "Want me to sit with you while you make that call?"
steps.expect: one real offer they can accept with a single word (`daily/social/host-a-guest-at-home`'s food instinct often applies).

steps.action: **Close with continuity, and mean it.** "I'll check on you Thursday." Then check on them Thursday. Distress outlives the sympathy window; the second and third check-ins are worth more than the first.
steps.expect: a follow-up promised at a named time, and a reminder set so it happens.

recipes.verification: They talked (or chose quiet) at their own pace, heard validation and no minimizers, received one concrete offer, and a follow-up happened at the named time. The honest metric arrives later: they come to you the next time it is heavy.

recipes.title: congratulate a new parent
recipes.name: congratulate-a-new-parent
recipes.goal: Congratulate a new parent in a way that makes their life easier, respects recovery and bonding, and avoids adding hosting work to an already full season.

steps.action: **Send a short warm message.** Say congratulations, name the baby if the name has been shared, and keep it low-demand: "No need to reply."
steps.expect: the parent receives care without another task.

steps.action: **Do not visit unannounced.** Ask once, or wait for an invitation. Hospitals and homes are not open houses after birth or placement.
steps.expect: the parent controls access to their space and baby.

steps.action: **Offer practical help over cute gifts.** Suggest one useful action: meal drop, grocery run, dog walk, laundry pickup, sibling outing, pharmacy errand, or coffee delivery.
steps.expect: the offer solves a real problem.

steps.action: **Make the offer specific.** Instead of "Let me know," say "I can drop dinner Tuesday at 5, no visit, just porch handoff. Any allergies?" [BRANCH: meal drop | errand help] choose meal drop if you know food needs; choose errands if you do not.
steps.expect: they can answer yes, no, or allergy details with little effort.

steps.action: **Respect the doorway.** If dropping food, label it, include reheating notes, text when it is outside, and leave unless invited in.
steps.expect: the parent receives food without cleaning, dressing, or hosting.

steps.action: **Compliment without evaluating.** Say the baby is beautiful, the family looks loved, or you are happy for them. Avoid comments about body, feeding, sleep choices, or whether they look tired.
steps.expect: your words do not open a parenting debate.

steps.action: **Ask before sharing photos or news.** ⚠️ *Irreversible:* once baby photos, names, or birth details are posted, privacy cannot be fully restored.
steps.expect: nothing appears online or in group chats without parent permission.

steps.action: **Follow up after the first rush.** Check in two or four weeks later with another concrete offer.
steps.expect: support continues after the announcement attention fades.

recipes.verification: The parent received a warm message, no unannounced visit, one specific practical offer, and no shared baby information without permission.

recipes.title: congratulate someone
recipes.name: congratulate-someone
recipes.goal: Someone receives a timely, sincere congratulations that recognizes their achievement without stealing focus or adding awkward comparison.

steps.action: **Act while it is fresh.** Send the message the same day if possible, or soon after you learn the news.
steps.expect: the congratulations feels connected to the moment.

steps.action: **Choose the medium.** [BRANCH: close relationship | professional or public relationship] call, voice note, or personal text for closeness, or email, card, comment, or chat for formal contexts.
steps.expect: the medium matches the relationship.

steps.action: **Name the achievement specifically.** Say the promotion, graduation, award, new baby, launch, move, recovery, or milestone.
steps.expect: they can tell you noticed the real event.

steps.action: **Add one sincere detail.** Mention effort, persistence, taste, kindness, courage, skill, or the impact you saw.
steps.expect: the message sounds personal rather than copied.

steps.action: **Keep comparisons out.** Do not mention who failed, who is jealous, how long it took, or how you would have done it.
steps.expect: the focus stays on their good news.

steps.action: **Match the energy.** [BRANCH: big life event | modest win] use warmth and celebration, or a concise "well done" with a specific note.
steps.expect: the tone feels supportive, not inflated or flat.

steps.action: **Offer a next step only if real.** Suggest coffee, a toast, help celebrating, or a small gift only if you intend to follow through.
steps.expect: any offer creates no false obligation.

steps.action: **Send and let them receive it.** Avoid adding corrections, advice, or your own news in the same message.
steps.expect: the final message is clean and centered on them.

recipes.verification: The sent message names the achievement, includes a sincere specific note, matches the relationship, and contains no comparison, advice, or privacy breach.

recipes.title: deal with a difficult coworker
recipes.name: deal-with-a-difficult-coworker
recipes.goal: Handle a coworker problem by documenting facts, addressing behavior directly when appropriate, and escalating through the right work channel if it continues.

steps.action: **Write down facts promptly.** Record date, time, location, people present, behavior, and work impact.
steps.expect: you have a factual note, not a vent.

steps.action: **Check the pattern.** [BRANCH: one-off irritation | repeated or serious behavior] Decide whether direct repair is enough or documentation should continue.
steps.expect: the response matches the severity.

steps.action: **Clarify expectations.** Identify what behavior needs to change, such as deadlines, tone, interruptions, or handoffs.
steps.expect: you can state the ask in one sentence.

steps.action: **Address it directly first when safe.** Say, "When X happens, Y is blocked. I need Z going forward."
steps.expect: the focus stays on behavior and impact.

steps.action: **Confirm agreements in writing.** Send a brief follow-up with decisions, owners, and dates.
steps.expect: there is a shared record.

steps.action: **Keep documenting repeats.** Note new incidents and any attempts to resolve them. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* do not secretly record audio or share private HR details unless company policy and local law allow it.
steps.expect: escalation evidence is organized.

steps.action: **Escalate to your manager.** Bring facts, impact, what you tried, and what help you need.
steps.expect: the manager receives an actionable workplace issue.

steps.action: **Use HR or formal channels for harassment, discrimination, threats, or retaliation.** Do not manage serious misconduct alone.
steps.expect: the issue reaches the channel responsible for risk.

recipes.verification: You have factual documentation, made a direct behavior-focused request when safe, and escalated through manager or HR channels if the conduct continued or was serious.

recipes.title: decline a request from your boss
recipes.name: decline-a-request-from-your-boss
recipes.goal: Decline or renegotiate a request from your boss while being honest about capacity and keeping alignment on priorities.

steps.action: **Clarify the ask.** Restate the deliverable, deadline, and quality bar in your own words.
steps.expect: your boss can confirm what is being requested.

steps.action: **Check real capacity.** Compare the request against your current deadlines, meetings, energy, and commitments.
steps.expect: you know what would be delayed or reduced.

steps.action: **Acknowledge the importance.** Start with the business reason or urgency instead of a flat refusal.
steps.expect: your response shows you heard the request.

steps.action: **State the constraint honestly.** Say what prevents you from taking it on as requested, using specific workload or timing facts.
steps.expect: the capacity issue is concrete rather than vague.

steps.action: **Offer alternatives.** [BRANCH: reprioritize | reduce scope | delegate | extend deadline] Suggest one or two workable paths.
steps.expect: your boss has options to choose from.

steps.action: **Ask for priority alignment.** Ask which task should move if this new request is more important.
steps.expect: tradeoffs are explicit.

steps.action: **Confirm the decision in writing.** Send a brief note with the chosen priority, deadline, and any work you will not do.
steps.expect: both sides have the same record.

steps.action: **Follow through on the agreed path.** Start the selected option or hand off the declined work cleanly.
steps.expect: the work plan changes without ambiguity.

steps.action: **Avoid hidden refusal.** Do not silently accept and then miss the deadline. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* lost trust is hard to repair; raise the conflict before the deadline passes.
steps.expect: the issue is visible while there is still time to adjust.

recipes.verification: Your boss has confirmed which request, deadline, scope, or existing priority changes, and that decision is captured in writing.

recipes.title: decline an invitation politely
recipes.name: decline-an-invitation-politely
recipes.goal: An invitation you cannot or do not want to accept is declined promptly and warmly, keeping the relationship intact and your calendar honest, without a fabricated excuse waiting to unravel.

steps.action: **Reply promptly, by the invitation's own channel.** A fast no is a courtesy; a late no costs the host planning options. Formal invitations with RSVP mechanics get the mechanic used (`communication/schedule-a-meeting`'s decline button exists for this).
steps.expect: a response within a day or two of deciding, not at the reminder.

steps.action: **Thank first, and mean it.** "Thanks for thinking of me" is true even when the answer is no; being invited is a small gift.
steps.expect: warmth up front, so the no lands on a cushion.

steps.action: **Decline clearly, without a fog of maybes.** "I can't make it" or "I'm going to pass on this one." Clear beats soft-but-ambiguous ("I'll try to swing by"), which the host must interpret and cater for.
steps.expect: a no the host can plan around.

steps.action: **Give a reason only at the honesty level you can sustain.** A true brief reason is fine ("we have family visiting"); no reason is also fine ("I can't make it that night" is complete). Fabricated specifics are the trap: they demand memory and invite follow-up questions.
steps.expect: nothing said tonight that becomes a lie by Saturday.

steps.action: **Signal the relationship's future, matched to which no this is.** This-time-no: attach a real alternative ("gutted to miss it; can we grab lunch next week?") and then actually propose it. This-kind-no: warmth without a counter-offer, so the pattern quietly ends.
steps.expect: the follow-up matches your actual intent; fake "let's do something soon" is the small lie that erodes.

steps.action: **Close warm and wish the event well.** "Hope it's a great one; send photos."
steps.expect: the exchange ends with the relationship exactly where it was or better.

recipes.verification: The host got a prompt, clear, warm no through the right channel, nothing untrue was said, the follow-up signal matched your real intent, any proposed alternative was actually pursued, and the next invitation's arrival (or intentional non-arrival) matches what you wanted.

recipes.title: end a conversation gracefully
recipes.name: end-a-conversation-gracefully
recipes.goal: The conversation ends within a few minutes, both people feel the exchange was complete, and the other person is left with a warm final impression rather than the sense of being escaped from.

steps.action: **Wait for a natural seam.** Let the current thought finish: a laugh, a story landing, a brief pause. Do not cut someone off mid-sentence to leave.
steps.expect: a beat of silence or a topic that has clearly resolved.

steps.action: **Deploy a bridge phrase.** Signal the ending before it happens: "Before I let you go...", "I should wrap up in a minute, but first...", or "One last thing I wanted to ask you." The bridge gives the other person a few seconds to adjust.
steps.expect: their posture or tone shifts to wrap-up mode; nobody is surprised by what comes next.

steps.action: **State a concrete exit.** Name the real, specific thing you are doing next: "I need to catch Maria before she leaves", "I'm going to grab food before they clear it", "I have a call at the top of the hour." Vague exits ("well, anyway...") stall; concrete ones move.
steps.expect: the reason lands as information, not rejection.

steps.action: **Close warm with a specific callback.** Reference something they actually said: "Good luck with the kitchen renovation", "I'm going to try that podcast you mentioned." Use their name if you have it. [BRANCH: you want future contact → add one concrete follow-up ("I'll email you that article tonight") | you don't → keep it to the warm callback alone, no fake "let's get coffee"]
steps.expect: a smile or reciprocal closing line from them.

steps.action: **Physically leave on the close.** Handshake, wave, or step away immediately after the closing line. Lingering after a goodbye restarts the conversation.
steps.expect: you are three steps away within seconds of the last word.

recipes.verification: The conversation is over, you have physically moved on to the stated next thing, the other person got a specific personal callback in the final exchange, and no goodbye was said more than twice.

recipes.title: end a relationship kindly
recipes.name: end-a-relationship-kindly
recipes.goal: End a romantic relationship clearly and compassionately, without cruelty, false hope, or avoidable confusion.

steps.action: **Choose the safest respectful channel.** [BRANCH: safe relationship | unsafe or volatile relationship] Meet in person if possible; use phone, text, or support if safety requires distance.
steps.expect: the channel balances respect and safety.

steps.action: **Prepare one clear sentence.** "I care about you, and I am ending our relationship."
steps.expect: the message cannot be mistaken for a negotiation.

steps.action: **Say it early.** Do not build a long preamble that makes them guess.
steps.expect: they know the conversation's purpose.

steps.action: **Be honest without being cruel.** Name the real broad reason, such as compatibility, trust, or wanting different futures, without listing every flaw.
steps.expect: the truth is clear but not weaponized.

steps.action: **Do not be wishy-washy.** Avoid "maybe someday" unless you genuinely mean a defined pause.
steps.expect: the ending is understandable.

steps.action: **Allow their reaction.** They may cry, go quiet, ask questions, or be angry. Listen without surrendering the decision.
steps.expect: their feelings have space, but the decision remains intact.

steps.action: **Set immediate logistics.** Discuss leaving, belongings, contact, shared plans, and who tells whom. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* do not use threats, public humiliation, outing, or disclosure of private information to force the ending.
steps.expect: the next 24-72 hours are practical.

steps.action: **Leave cleanly.** Repeat the core sentence if needed, then end the conversation rather than relitigating all history.
steps.expect: the breakup has an actual close.

recipes.verification: The other person has heard that the relationship is over, the reason was stated without cruelty, immediate logistics were addressed, and no false hope was offered.

recipes.title: give a compliment
recipes.name: give-a-compliment
recipes.goal: A genuine compliment delivered so it lands: specific, sincere, well-timed, and free of hooks, leaving the receiver a little taller and the relationship a little warmer.

steps.action: **Catch the specific, not the general.** "Great job" evaporates; "the way you handled that interruption without losing the thread was impressive" sticks, because specificity is the proof you actually paid attention.
steps.expect: a compliment containing at least one concrete detail only a genuine observer would have.

steps.action: **Compliment choices and effort over lottery tickets.** What someone did, made, or chose ("that color combination", "the patience you showed", "this sauce") lands better than what they were born with; effort-praise also survives repetition.
steps.expect: the content pointing at something they can feel ownership of.

steps.action: **Deliver it clean, with a period at the end.** No hook ("...so could you help me move Saturday?"), no comparison that demotes someone else ("unlike Tom's version"), no softener that retracts it ("not bad for a beginner"). Say it, stop, let it exist.
steps.expect: a complete sentence of pure credit, followed by silence or a normal topic, not a request.

steps.action: **Match the register to the relationship and setting.** Colleagues: work-adjacent and public-safe ("your write-up made the decision easy"). Strangers: light and exit-friendly ("great dog, great coat"). Appearance compliments: safest about choices (glasses, jacket, haircut `daily/errands/get-a-haircut` results included) and calibrated to context; when in doubt, compliment the work, not the body.
steps.expect: nothing that would read differently on a loudspeaker.

steps.action: **Consider the upgrade: compliment them to their boss, their partner, or behind their back.** Relayed praise ("your colleague told me you saved that project") is the highest-value form, and back-channel kindness has a way of arriving.
steps.expect: where stakes or shyness make direct praise awkward, the indirect route delivering it better.

steps.action: **Receive their response gracefully.** They may deflect ("oh, it was nothing"); reaffirm once, lightly ("well, it worked on me"), and move on. Do not force them to accept it ceremonially.
steps.expect: the moment closing warm and unlabored.

recipes.verification: The compliment was specific, hook-free, register-matched, and delivered with a period; the receiver's day visibly ticked upward; and nothing about it would embarrass either of you replayed aloud.

recipes.title: give a eulogy
recipes.name: give-a-eulogy
recipes.goal: Deliver a brief, truthful eulogy that helps mourners remember the person with love, without pretending they were perfect or making the service about your grief.

steps.action: **Choose one theme.** Pick a sentence that can hold the eulogy: "She made people feel expected," "He repaired what others threw away," or "They loved by showing up."
steps.expect: every story you choose can point back to that theme.

steps.action: **Gather a few stories.** Select two or three short stories from different parts of their life, including one small everyday detail. Ask close family if any story is off-limits.
steps.expect: the eulogy shows a full person through concrete moments.

steps.action: **Honor, do not perfect.** Name complexity gently if needed: "Life with him was not always easy, and his love was still real." Avoid score-settling, public revelations, or forced sainthood.
steps.expect: mourners hear truth without feeling ambushed.

steps.action: **Keep it short.** Aim for 3 to 5 minutes, about 450 to 700 spoken words. Cut anything that exists mainly to explain your relationship to the deceased.
steps.expect: the eulogy can be read slowly without rushing the service.

steps.action: **Make an emotion plan.** Print the eulogy in large type, mark pauses, bring water, and ask one person to stand ready to finish if you cannot. [BRANCH: continue | hand off] continue after a breath if words return; hand off if you cannot speak.
steps.expect: tears are allowed without the service losing its path.

steps.action: **Practice aloud once, then stop polishing.** Read it standing, with the first and last sentences exactly as written. Do not keep revising into the night.
steps.expect: your voice has met the hardest lines before the service.

steps.action: **Deliver to the room slowly.** Start with your name and relationship, then the theme, stories, and a final line of gratitude or farewell. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* public accusations, secrets, and family conflicts cannot be unsaid at a funeral, so remove them before speaking.
steps.expect: the room has room to grieve, smile, and breathe.

steps.action: **Return the focus after speaking.** Step away, sit down, and let the service continue. Save extra memories for the reception or condolence line.
steps.expect: the eulogy closes cleanly instead of becoming a second service.

recipes.verification: The eulogy has one clear theme, two or three approved stories, a 3 to 5 minute length, and a backup reader or printed copy ready.

recipes.title: give a good handshake
recipes.name: give-a-good-handshake
recipes.goal: A handshake feels respectful, brief, and confident without crushing, lingering, or ignoring cultural context.

steps.action: **Read the cue.** Notice whether the other person extends a hand or leaves space.
steps.expect: you know whether to offer or skip contact.

steps.action: **Offer at chest height.** Extend your right hand with thumb up and palm angled sideways.
steps.expect: the gesture is easy to meet.

steps.action: **Connect web-to-web.** Slide hands until the web between thumb and index finger meets theirs.
steps.expect: palms align instead of catching fingers only.

steps.action: **Grip firmly, not hard.** Close fingers with moderate pressure.
steps.expect: the hand feels held, not squeezed.

steps.action: **Use two pumps.** Move hands once or twice from the elbow, then stop.
steps.expect: the shake is brief and controlled.

steps.action: **Make natural eye contact.** Look at the person while greeting them by name if known.
steps.expect: attention is on the person, not the hands.

steps.action: **Release cleanly.** Let go as the pumps end and return your hand to your side.
steps.expect: neither person has to pull away.

steps.action: **Adapt respectfully.** [BRANCH: handshake accepted | handshake declined] continue normally or switch to a nod and greeting.
steps.expect: the interaction stays comfortable.

recipes.verification: The handshake includes web-to-web contact, moderate pressure, one or two pumps, eye contact, and a clean release.

recipes.title: give a toast
recipes.name: give-a-toast
recipes.goal: A short toast delivered at a dinner, wedding, or send-off that lands warm, earns one genuine laugh or one genuine mist of the eyes, and ends before anyone checks the time — the whole craft being that it is about them, not you.

steps.action: **Claim the room gently.** Stand if the group is larger than a table's worth, raise the glass to shoulder height, and use the opener that always works: "If I could have everyone for just a moment." Wait out the settling; starting over chatter buries the first line.
steps.expect: faces turned, conversations paused, your glass visibly the flag.

steps.action: **Run the three-part formula: connection, story, wish.** One line on who you are to the honoree ("I've sat next to Ana for six years of Mondays"); one *short specific* story or trait that only you would tell, aimed at their best qualities ("the year my project collapsed, she rebuilt my spreadsheet and my morale, in that order"); one forward-looking wish ("here's to the next chapter being even kinder to her than she is to everyone else").
steps.expect: 60 to 90 seconds total; the story concrete enough to be about no one else on earth.

steps.action: **Aim the warmth, not the roast.** One gentle tease is seasoning; embarrassment, in-jokes the room cannot parse, exes, and anything the honoree would wince at are banned regardless of how funny the memory is to you. The test: would they be glad their grandmother heard it?
steps.expect: the honoree smiling at their own story, not surviving it.

steps.action: **Land the ending cleanly.** Signal the close ("So please raise your glasses—"), deliver the wish in one sentence, name them ("—to Ana!"), and drink. The named toast is the period; do not resume talking after it.
steps.expect: the room echoing the name, glasses up, a clean end.

steps.action: **Clink and eye-contact per local custom, then sit down.** Sitting down promptly is the second most appreciated part of any toast.
steps.expect: the moment returned to the table; the honoree's thanks caught with a nod, not a second speech.

recipes.verification: Under two minutes, three parts present, the story specific to the honoree, nothing they would wince at, ended on their name with glasses raised, and you sat down while the room still wanted one more sentence.

recipes.title: give constructive feedback
recipes.name: give-constructive-feedback
recipes.goal: The other person understands exactly which behavior you are flagging and why it matters, agrees on a concrete change going forward, and the relationship is intact or stronger afterward.

steps.action: **Prepare one specific instance.** Write down the situation, the observable behavior, and its impact before you talk. One issue per conversation; a list of three becomes an indictment.
steps.expect: you can state the behavior in one sentence a video camera would have captured ("you interrupted the client twice"), not a trait ("you're dismissive").

steps.action: **Ask first.** "Do you have a few minutes? I'd like to share some feedback on yesterday's meeting. Is now okay?" The ask transfers a little control and takes the ambush out of it. [BRANCH: they say yes → proceed | they say not now → get a concrete time within a day or two, and hold it]
steps.expect: explicit consent and their attention, or a scheduled slot.

steps.action: **State the situation and behavior, factually.** "In yesterday's client call, when Sam was presenting the timeline, you cut in twice before he finished." No "always", no "never", no adjectives about them as a person.
steps.expect: they can locate the exact moment; a fact-check ("was it twice?") is fine, an identity defense means you drifted into character territory.

steps.action: **State the impact.** The consequence you observed or felt: "Sam lost his thread, and the client started directing questions only to you, which undercuts the team." Impact is what makes it feedback instead of a preference.
steps.expect: a shift in their face from defense to processing; this is usually the moment it lands.

steps.action: **Pause and genuinely listen.** Ask "how did it look from your side?" and then actually stop talking. Their context may change your read (maybe Sam asked them beforehand to jump in).
steps.expect: their account, which you can honestly engage with; feedback that survives their context is stronger, feedback that doesn't should be withdrawn on the spot.

steps.action: **Agree on the forward-looking change.** Co-author it: "What would work better next time?" beats dictating. Settle on one observable behavior ("let Sam finish sections, add your points at the transitions").
steps.expect: a specific next-time behavior both of you could verify, said back in their words.

steps.action: **Close with real regard.** One true sentence about why the feedback was worth giving: "I'm raising it because clients should see how good this team is." Skip the compliment sandwich; a bolted-on opening compliment teaches people to flinch at praise.
steps.expect: a normal-temperature end to the conversation, ideally with thanks.

recipes.verification: The other person can restate the specific behavior and its impact in their own words, a single forward-looking change was agreed and is observable, no character labels were used by either side, and a follow-up moment (if needed) has a date.

recipes.title: give directions
recipes.name: give-directions
recipes.goal: A person who asked the way leaves with directions they can actually follow — or with an honest referral to a better source.

steps.action: **Confirm the destination and their mode.** "The central library — walking or driving?" Mode changes the route (one-ways, shortcuts, distance tolerance).
steps.expect: destination and mode pinned; if the name is ambiguous ("the Starbucks" — which?), disambiguate now.

steps.action: **Honestly gate yourself.** [BRANCH: you know it cold → step 3 | you half-know → say so and offer only the certain part | no idea → "I'm not sure — sorry" and suggest maps/a shop to ask] A confident wrong answer costs them 20 minutes; "I don't know" costs seconds.
steps.expect: you're only proceeding on solid knowledge.

steps.action: **Orient them physically first.** Turn them the right way before any words: "So, facing this way—" (gesture down the street). Directions given against their current facing fail at the first turn.
steps.expect: their body points along leg one.

steps.action: **Give the route in 3 chunks maximum, landmark-anchored.** People hold ~3 instructions. "Straight to the church (2 blocks) — left there — it's on your right past the pharmacy." Landmarks beat street names for strangers; distances in blocks/minutes beat meters.
steps.expect: a route of ≤3 legs, each ending at something visible/checkable.

steps.action: **Give the overshoot tell.** "If you reach the river, you've gone too far."
steps.expect: they have a failure detector, not just a plan.

steps.action: **Have them confirm the first leg back to you.** "So I go...?" or simply watch that they set off the right way; re-anchor if the readback is off.
steps.expect: correct readback or correct departure heading.

recipes.verification: They departed along the correct first leg carrying ≤3 landmark-anchored instructions and an overshoot tell — or they left with an honest "don't know" and a better source instead of a guess.

recipes.title: greet a neighbor
recipes.name: greet-a-neighbor
recipes.goal: A neighbor encounter — hallway, elevator, sidewalk, or a first meeting after moving in — ends with goodwill maintained or built, in proportion to what both people wanted from it.

steps.action: **Read the encounter's size.** [BRANCH: passing at distance → nod/wave/"morning" | shared confined wait (elevator, laundry room) → greeting + optional small exchange | first meeting after a move → introduction, see step 4]
steps.expect: you've matched your opener to the container — a passing nod needs no conversation; a 40-second elevator ride tolerates one.

steps.action: **Deliver the greeting with eye contact and a smile.** "Morning." / "Hi." / a raised-hand wave across the street. That's a complete, successful interaction by itself.
steps.expect: acknowledgment returned — nod, greeting, smile.

steps.action: **Optionally extend one beat — and read the response.** One low-stakes line: weather, the building ("elevator's back, finally"), their dog. Their answer's length tells you everything: short + closed → warm exit ("have a good one"); engaged → a brief chat is welcome.
steps.expect: conversation sized to the least-interested participant, ending on time.

steps.action: **First-meeting version: introduce with name + unit.** "Hi — I'm Sam, just moved into 3B." Offer a handshake where that's local custom. Reciprocal intro usually follows; a practical question makes a natural second beat ("Is Tuesday really bin day?").
steps.expect: names exchanged; you can now greet by name forever, which compounds.

steps.action: **Bank the details.** Name, unit/house, dog's name, anything they mentioned. Next encounter opens with it ("How was the trip?").
steps.expect: recorded (mentally or literally); future greetings get warmer at zero cost.

recipes.verification: The encounter ended at or above its starting warmth, sized to what both parties wanted, and (first meetings) you can address them by name next time.

recipes.title: handle a rude comment
recipes.name: handle-a-rude-comment
recipes.goal: Respond to a rude comment without escalating unnecessarily or surrendering your dignity.

steps.action: **Pause first.** Take one breath before answering, even if you know what you want to say.
steps.expect: the first response is chosen, not reflexive.

steps.action: **Check the stakes.** Decide whether the comment affects safety, work, reputation, or only annoyance.
steps.expect: your response matches the setting.

steps.action: **Choose an option.** [BRANCH: ignore | name it | question it] pick the lightest response that protects you.
steps.expect: you have a clear lane before speaking.

steps.action: **Ignore cleanly if it is bait.** Let the comment pass and redirect to the task or another person.
steps.expect: the rude person gets no reward from your reaction.

steps.action: **Name it if a boundary is needed.** Say "That was rude" or "Do not speak to me that way" in a calm tone.
steps.expect: the behavior is identified without a speech.

steps.action: **Question it if clarity helps.** Ask "What do you mean by that?" or "Can you say that another way?"
steps.expect: they must either soften, explain, or own the comment.

steps.action: **Return to the point.** Move back to the task, conversation, or next action.
steps.expect: you do not get trapped in a side argument.

steps.action: **Exit if it continues.** End the conversation, leave the room, mute the thread, or involve a moderator or manager.
steps.expect: contact with the rude behavior decreases.

recipes.verification: After the exchange, you have either ignored, named, questioned, or exited in a way that reduces harm and preserves your boundary.

recipes.title: handle a school conflict
recipes.name: handle-a-school-conflict
recipes.goal: Help a child address a school conflict with safety, fairness, documentation, and appropriate adult support.

steps.action: **Listen privately.** Ask what happened, who was involved, where it happened, and what the child needs now.
steps.expect: the child feels heard and basic facts are clearer.

steps.action: **Assess safety.** Check for threats, injury, bullying, discrimination, harassment, or self-harm concerns.
steps.expect: urgent issues are separated from ordinary conflict.

steps.action: **Document facts.** Write dates, locations, messages, screenshots, witnesses, and prior attempts to solve it.
steps.expect: details are preserved accurately.

steps.action: **Choose the first contact.** Email or speak with the teacher, counselor, coach, or administrator closest to the issue.
steps.expect: the school has a clear concise report.

steps.action: **Coach the child.** Practice a respectful statement, boundary, or request if direct repair is safe.
steps.expect: the child has words for their part of the solution.

steps.action: **Follow up.** Ask what action was taken and watch whether the conflict stops.
steps.expect: the plan is monitored instead of assumed.

recipes.verification: The conflict has a documented summary, the appropriate school adult has been contacted, and the child knows the current safety or repair plan.

recipes.title: handle a tense family dinner
recipes.name: handle-a-tense-family-dinner
recipes.goal: Get through a tense family dinner with your dignity intact, fewer escalations, and a clear exit plan if the evening stops being tolerable.

steps.action: **Set your boundary in advance.** Choose a sentence you can repeat: "I'm not discussing my dating life tonight" or "I'm here for dinner, not a political debate."
steps.expect: you have words ready before adrenaline arrives.

steps.action: **Enter with one neutral contribution.** Bring a side dish, help set the table, ask about travel, or compliment the food.
steps.expect: the first impression is cooperative, not defensive.

steps.action: **Use safe topics early.** Ask about recipes, kids, pets, local events, sports, movies, house projects, or old family stories that do not start fights.
steps.expect: conversation has somewhere to go besides the usual conflict lane.

steps.action: **Redirect at the first hook.** When someone pokes the boundary, answer once and move: "I'm not getting into that tonight. How was your trip?" [BRANCH: direct redirect | softer redirect] use direct for repeat offenders; use softer when someone simply forgot.
steps.expect: the topic changes or the pattern becomes visible.

steps.action: **Take the bathroom break.** If your body heats up, excuse yourself, breathe, text a grounding person, or wash your hands slowly.
steps.expect: you return with enough distance to choose your next sentence.

steps.action: **Do not take the bait.** Refuse insults disguised as questions, old grievances, or "everyone knows" traps. Short lines work: "I see it differently," "I'm not debating this here," "Pass the potatoes?"
steps.expect: you give less fuel than the provocation requests.

steps.action: **Leave before the exit becomes dramatic.** If the boundary keeps being crossed, thank the host and go. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* shouted accusations at a family table can echo for years, so leave before you say the sentence you came to avoid.
steps.expect: you are out of the room before the worst version of the fight.

steps.action: **Debrief later, not in the driveway group text.** Write down what happened, what worked, and what boundary you need next time.
steps.expect: the next plan is based on evidence, not only exhaustion.

recipes.verification: You stated or upheld at least one topic boundary, used a redirect or break before escalating, and left or stayed by choice rather than pressure.

recipes.title: handle a toddler tantrum
recipes.name: handle-a-toddler-tantrum
recipes.goal: Get through a toddler tantrum safely while holding the boundary, naming the feeling, and reconnecting after the storm passes.

steps.action: **Check safety first.** Move the child away from traffic, stairs, sharp objects, hot surfaces, or breakable items.
steps.expect: the tantrum can continue without immediate physical danger.

steps.action: **Lower your voice and body.** Speak slowly, unclench your hands, and get near the child's level without crowding them.
steps.expect: you are not adding more intensity to the room.

steps.action: **Acknowledge the feeling.** Say the feeling and the limit in one short phrase, such as "You are mad. I will not let you hit."
steps.expect: the child hears that the feeling is accepted and the unsafe behavior is not.

steps.action: **Hold the boundary.** Do not give the denied item or cancel the required transition because of screaming.
steps.expect: the rule stays the same without a long debate.

steps.action: **Offer a small choice.** [BRANCH: choice accepted | choice ignored] give two acceptable options, such as walk or be carried, blue cup or green cup.
steps.expect: the child has control inside the boundary.

steps.action: **Use few words.** Repeat the same calm limit if needed and stop explaining once the child is too upset to process language.
steps.expect: the conflict does not grow through negotiation.

steps.action: **Block unsafe behavior.** Hold hands gently away from hitting, move objects, or carry the child if leaving is required. ⚠️ *Irreversible:* never shake, throw, or strike a child, because injury and fear cannot be undone.
steps.expect: everyone remains physically safe.

steps.action: **Wait for the wave to pass.** Stay nearby if safe, or give space while watching, and let crying slow before teaching.
steps.expect: breathing, volume, and body tension start to come down.

steps.action: **Reconnect after.** Offer comfort, restate the limit briefly, and guide the next action without a lecture.
steps.expect: the child can rejoin the day and knows the relationship is intact.

recipes.verification: The child and others are safe, the core boundary was held, and the child has reconnected or moved to a calmer next activity.

recipes.title: handle a tween mood swing
recipes.name: handle-a-tween-mood-swing
recipes.goal: Help a tween move through a mood swing while preserving connection, boundaries, and growing independence.

steps.action: **Check safety and privacy.** Move the conversation away from siblings, peers, or public attention.
steps.expect: the tween is less exposed and easier to reach.

steps.action: **Name the shift gently.** Say you notice a hard moment without accusing them of being dramatic.
steps.expect: the tween feels observed rather than attacked.

steps.action: **Offer space or support.** Ask whether they want quiet, a walk, food, help, or a few minutes alone.
steps.expect: the tween gets some control over regulation.

steps.action: **Hold basic limits.** Keep rules against insults, threats, slamming near people, or unsafe behavior.
steps.expect: feelings are allowed and harm is not.

steps.action: **Return when calmer.** Discuss the trigger, repair, or plan after intensity drops.
steps.expect: problem-solving happens when the tween can think.

steps.action: **Watch patterns.** Notice sleep, hunger, screens, school stress, friendship issues, puberty changes, and frequency.
steps.expect: repeated triggers become visible.

recipes.verification: The tween is safe, intensity has decreased, the boundary remains clear, and a later repair or trigger discussion is planned or completed.

recipes.title: handle picky eating
recipes.name: handle-picky-eating
recipes.goal: Reduce mealtime conflict while helping a child gradually accept a wider range of foods.

steps.action: **Set the adult job.** Decide what food is offered, where meals happen, and when the meal ends.
steps.expect: the meal has clear structure.

steps.action: **Set the child job.** Let the child decide whether and how much to eat from what is served.
steps.expect: pressure drops and appetite cues stay respected.

steps.action: **Serve one safe food.** Put one familiar accepted item beside small portions of family food.
steps.expect: the child has something available without a separate rescue meal.

steps.action: **Use tiny exposures.** Invite looking, smelling, touching, licking, or one small taste without requiring swallowing.
steps.expect: new food becomes less threatening over time.

steps.action: **Keep language neutral.** Avoid bribing, shaming, or labeling the child as picky during the meal.
steps.expect: attention shifts away from power struggles.

steps.action: **Review patterns weekly.** Track accepted foods, refused textures, constipation, fatigue, and growth concerns.
steps.expect: you can distinguish normal selectiveness from a bigger issue.

recipes.verification: Meals follow a predictable structure, the child has one accepted option, and at least one low-pressure exposure to a nonpreferred food happens without coercion.

recipes.title: handle sibling fights
recipes.name: handle-sibling-fights
recipes.goal: Stop a sibling fight safely, help each child regulate, and guide repair without taking sides too quickly.

steps.action: **Stop harm first.** Move bodies apart, remove thrown objects, and block hitting or biting.
steps.expect: no one can keep hurting another person.

steps.action: **Use neutral language.** Say what you see without deciding the whole story immediately.
steps.expect: both children hear that safety comes before blame.

steps.action: **Separate to calm.** Give each child space, water, breathing, or quiet time while staying nearby as needed.
steps.expect: volume and body tension start to drop.

steps.action: **Hear each child briefly.** Ask each child what happened and what they needed, one at a time.
steps.expect: the adult has enough information to guide repair.

steps.action: **Set the boundary.** State the rule about bodies, belongings, words, or shared space.
steps.expect: the limit is clear and applies to everyone.

steps.action: **Repair and reset.** Help return an item, apologize, make a plan, or separate activities for now.
steps.expect: the conflict has a next step instead of a winner.

recipes.verification: The children are physically safe, the immediate conflict has stopped, and each child knows the repair or separation plan.

recipes.title: have a difficult conversation
recipes.name: have-a-difficult-conversation
recipes.goal: A hard topic is raised with care, heard with less defensiveness, and closed with a clear outcome or next step.

steps.action: **Prepare the point.** Write the main concern, one concrete example, and what you hope changes.
steps.expect: you can explain the conversation without a speech.

steps.action: **Pick the time and place.** Choose privacy, enough time, and a setting where both people can leave or pause.
steps.expect: the context supports attention rather than performance.

steps.action: **Open with care and clarity.** Say why the relationship or work matters, then name the topic directly.
steps.expect: the other person knows this is serious but not an ambush.

steps.action: **Describe facts before interpretations.** Use dates, behaviors, or words you observed, then explain the impact.
steps.expect: the discussion starts from shared reality.

steps.action: **Listen for their account.** Ask what you are missing, let them finish, and reflect the part you understand.
steps.expect: they have a real chance to respond.

steps.action: **Make the request specific.** [BRANCH: ask for change | share a boundary] Ask for a behavior if collaboration is possible; state a boundary if the behavior must stop.
steps.expect: the desired outcome is not vague.

steps.action: **Agree an outcome.** Decide who will do what by when, or agree that no agreement was reached and what happens next.
steps.expect: the close has a recordable result.

steps.action: **Avoid public damage.** ⚠️ *Irreversible:* humiliation, threats, and private disclosures can permanently change trust, so do not use an audience as leverage.
steps.expect: the conversation stays as private as the situation allows.

steps.action: **Follow up briefly.** Send a short note if stakes are practical, or check in later if stakes are relational.
steps.expect: the outcome survives beyond the moment.

recipes.verification: At the end, both people know the topic, the impact, and the agreed outcome or next step.

recipes.title: help a child manage big emotions
recipes.name: help-a-child-manage-big-emotions
recipes.goal: Help a child move through anger, fear, sadness, or overwhelm with safety, connection, and a simple regulation plan.

steps.action: **Make the space safe.** Move sharp objects, separate kids who might hurt each other, and lower noise or crowding.
steps.expect: the child has room to be upset without causing harm.

steps.action: **Get low and use few words.** Speak calmly at the child's level and name what you see: "You are really mad."
steps.expect: the child hears connection rather than a lecture.

steps.action: **Validate the feeling, not unsafe behavior.** Say the feeling is allowed while holding the limit on hitting, throwing, or running away.
steps.expect: the child knows both the emotion and boundary are real.

steps.action: **Offer a regulation choice.** [BRANCH: comfort | space | movement] offer a hug, quiet corner, breathing, wall pushes, water, or a short walk.
steps.expect: the child can choose one next action or reject fewer options.

steps.action: **Wait out the peak.** Stay nearby, reduce demands, and repeat the limit only when needed.
steps.expect: crying, yelling, or shutdown begins to decrease.

steps.action: **Reconnect before problem-solving.** After the child calms, briefly describe what happened and ask what would help next time.
steps.expect: the child can listen and answer in simple words.

steps.action: **Repair harm.** Help the child apologize, clean up, check on someone, or try again without making shame the lesson.
steps.expect: the child practices responsibility after regulation returns.

recipes.verification: The child is physically safe, intensity has decreased, a boundary was held, and one repair or next-time strategy was practiced after calm returned.

recipes.title: help a child with homework
recipes.name: help-a-child-with-homework
recipes.goal: Support a child through homework by setting up the conditions, guiding their thinking, and preserving the teacher's view of what the child can do.

steps.action: **Set the environment.** Clear the table, reduce screens or noise that are not part of the task, and put supplies within reach.
steps.expect: the child can start without searching for basics.

steps.action: **Read the assignment together.** Ask the child to explain what is due and what the teacher wants.
steps.expect: both of you can name the task in one sentence.

steps.action: **Choose the first piece.** Break the work into small parts, such as read directions, do problems 1 to 5, draft one paragraph, or review notes.
steps.expect: the child has a next action that feels possible.

steps.action: **Guide, do not take over.** Ask questions, model one similar example if needed, and have the child do the assigned item.
steps.expect: the child's marks, words, or reasoning remain their own.

steps.action: **Use short work blocks.** [BRANCH: continue | take a break] work for 10 to 20 minutes depending on age, then pause for movement, water, or a reset.
steps.expect: attention improves or at least stops getting worse.

steps.action: **Praise effort and strategy.** Name the behavior you want repeated, such as checking directions, trying a second method, or explaining a mistake.
steps.expect: the child hears what they controlled, not just whether the answer was right.

steps.action: **Check for understanding.** Ask the child to teach back one problem or explain the next step without your prompt.
steps.expect: you can tell whether they understand or are copying.

steps.action: **Stop before a meltdown.** If frustration rises, pause, mark the stuck place, and return after a short break or the next day if appropriate.
steps.expect: the child is not learning that homework equals a fight.

steps.action: **Pack and communicate.** Put completed work where it belongs and email the teacher if directions are unclear, the workload is consistently too much, or the child cannot do it without heavy help.
steps.expect: the assignment is ready or the teacher has useful information.

recipes.verification: The child can explain what was completed, the work is packed or submitted, and any unresolved confusion has been sent to the teacher.

recipes.title: help a kid make friends
recipes.name: help-a-kid-make-friends
recipes.goal: Help a child build friendships by practicing social skills, creating opportunities, and respecting their pace.

steps.action: **Ask what they want.** Find out whether the child wants one friend, a group, playdates, or less loneliness.
steps.expect: the goal belongs to the child.

steps.action: **Identify likely matches.** Look for shared interests, kind classmates, clubs, teams, neighbors, or family friends.
steps.expect: there are one or two realistic connection options.

steps.action: **Practice a small opener.** Role-play asking to join, giving a compliment, or inviting someone to an activity.
steps.expect: the child has a simple phrase ready.

steps.action: **Arrange low-pressure time.** Set up a short playdate, activity, club meeting, or shared task.
steps.expect: interaction has structure and an endpoint.

steps.action: **Coach during recovery.** Afterward, ask what felt good, awkward, or worth trying again.
steps.expect: the child reflects without feeling judged.

steps.action: **Repeat consistently.** Offer regular chances with the same children when possible.
steps.expect: familiarity can turn into friendship.

recipes.verification: The child has practiced one friendship skill and had or scheduled one low-pressure social opportunity aligned with their interests.

recipes.title: help a shy child
recipes.name: help-a-shy-child
recipes.goal: Support a shy child in social situations without shaming their temperament or forcing performance.

steps.action: **Accept the temperament.** Describe the child as warming up slowly rather than rude or broken.
steps.expect: the child is not shamed for needing time.

steps.action: **Preview the situation.** Explain who will be there, what will happen, and how long it may last.
steps.expect: uncertainty decreases before arrival.

steps.action: **Offer a small script.** Practice one greeting, question, or exit phrase the child can use.
steps.expect: the child has words ready if they choose to speak.

steps.action: **Stay nearby first.** Let the child observe from beside you before expecting interaction.
steps.expect: the child can scan the room and settle.

steps.action: **Praise brave behavior.** Name specific effort such as looking up, waving, or answering one question.
steps.expect: progress is recognized without demanding extroversion.

steps.action: **Plan the next exposure.** Choose another small social step for later.
steps.expect: confidence builds through repetition.

recipes.verification: The child completes one manageable social step while feeling respected, and the caregiver has a next gradual exposure planned.

recipes.title: help with a science fair project
recipes.name: help-with-a-science-fair-project
recipes.goal: Help a child complete a science fair project that is safe, honest, and clearly their own work.

steps.action: **Read the rules together.** Identify required question, hypothesis, procedure, data, display, and citation parts.
